text: If you would make Fortune your friend; when people say money is to be got here and money is to be got there, take no notice; mind your own business; stay where you are; and secure all you can get, without stirring.
author: Goldsmith

text: Writers of novels and romances in general bring a double loss on their readers—they rob them both of their time and money; representing men, manners, and things, that never have been, nor are likely to be; either confounding or perverting history and truth, inflating the mind, or committing violence upon the understanding.
author: Mary Wortley Montagu

text: There are few who, either by extraordinary endowment or favour of fortune, have enjoyed the opportunity of deciding what mode of life in especial they would wish to embrace.
author: Cic

text: No man is poor who does not think himself so. But if in a full fortune with impatience he desires more, he proclaims his wants and his beggarly condition.
author: Jeremy Taylor

text: Commerce is a game of skill, which every one cannot play, which few men can play well.
author: Emerson

text: No wise man should make known the loss of fortune, any malpractices in his house, his being cheated, or his having been disgraced.
author: Hitopadesa

text: To be, or not to be, that is the question; / Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer / The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, / Or to take up arms against a sea of troubles, / And, by opposing, end them.
author: Ham

text: True joy is a serene and sober motion; and they are miserably out, that take laughing for rejoicing; the seat of it is within, and there is no cheerfulness like the resolutions of a brave mind that has fortune under its feet.
author: Sen

text: We learn wisdom from failure much more than from success; we often discover what will do by finding out what will not do; and probably he who never made a mistake never made a discovery. Horne Tooke used to say of his studies in intellectual philosophy, that he had become all the better acquainted with the country through having had the good luck sometimes to lose his way.
author: Smiles

text: Judgments that are made on the wrong side of the danger amount to no more than an affectation of skill, without either credit or effect.
author: L'Estrange

text: Thus we play the fools with the time; and the spirits of the wise sit in the clouds, and mock us.
author: Hen. IV

text: Dependence goes somewhat against the grain of a generous mind; and it is no wonder, considering the unreasonable advantage which is often taken of the inequality of fortune.
author: Jeremy Collier

text: Human life is more governed by fortune than by reason.
author: Hume

text: What men usually say of misfortunes, that they never come alone, may with equal truth be said of good fortune; nay, of other circumstances which gather round us in a harmonious way, whether it arise from a kind of fatality, or that man has the power of attracting to himself things that are mutually related.
author: Goethe

text: Uprightness, judgment, and sympathy with others will profit thee at every time and in every place.
author: Goethe

text: It is fortune, not wisdom, that rules man's life.
author: Cic

text: Let thy great deeds force fate to change her mind; / He that courts fortune boldly, makes her kind.
author: Dryden

text: Life is a casket, not precious in itself, but valuable in proportion to what fortune, or industry, or virtue has placed within it.
author: Landor

text: Yield not thy neck / To fortune's yoke, but let thy dauntless mind / Still ride in triumph over all mischance.
author: Hen. VI

text: Wherefore ever ramble on? / For the good is lying near. / Fortune learn to seize alone, / For that Fortune's ever here.
author: Goethe

text: Learn that nonsense is none the less nonsense because it is in rhyme; and that rhyme without a purpose or a thought that has not been better expressed before is a public nuisance, only to be tolerated because it is good for trade.
author: C. Fitzhugh

text: Men are seldom blessed with good fortune and good sense at the same time.
author: Livy

text: The painter should grind his own colours; the architect work in the mason's yard with his men; the master-manufacturer be himself a more skilful operator than any man in his mills; and the distinction between one man and another be only in experience and skill, and the authority and wealth which these must naturally and justly obtain.
author: Ruskin

text: To plough and sow, to reap and mow, my father bred me early, / For one, he said, to labour bred, was a match for fortune fairly.
author: Burns

text: "One thing above all others," says Goethe, "I have never thought about thinking." What a thrift of thinking faculty there; thrift almost of itself equal to a fortune in these days.
author: Carlyle

text: Truth itself shall lose its credit, if delivered by a person that has none.
author: South

text: It is not want of good fortune, want of happiness, but want of wisdom that man has to dread.
author: Carlyle

text: They who have no other trade but seeking their fortune, need never hope to find her; coquette-like, she flies from her close pursuers, and at last fixes on the plodding mechanic who stays at home and minds his business.
author: Goldsmith

text: Wealth is the application of mind to nature; and the art of getting rich consists not in industry, much less in saving, but in a better order, in timeliness, in being at the right spot.
author: Emerson

text: To judge by the event is an error all abuse and all commit; for in every instance, courage, if crowned with success, is heroism; if clouded by defeat, temerity.
author: Colton

text: If we are wise, we may thank ourselves; if we are great, we must thank fortune.
author: Bulwer Lytton

text: The judgment of the world stands upon matter of fortune.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: The reason why we sometimes see that men of the greatest capacities are not rich, is either because they despise wealth in comparison of something else, or, at least, are not content to be getting an estate, unless they may do it in their own way, and at the same time enjoy all the pleasures and gratifications of life.
author: Eustace Budgell

text: We play the fools with the time, and the spirits of the wise sit in the clouds and mock us.
author: Hen. IV

text: Many people think of knowledge as of money. They would like knowledge, but cannot face the perseverance and self-denial that go to the acquisition of it.
author: John Morley

text: The man makes the circumstances, and is spiritually as well as economically the artificer of his own fortune, but the man's circumstances are the element he is appointed to live and work in; so that in a no less genuine sense it can be said circumstances make the man.
author: Carlyle

text: Leisure and solitude are the best effect of riches, because mother of thought. Both are avoided by most rich men, who seek company and business, which are signs of their being weary of themselves.
author: Sir W. Temple

text: Knowledge introduceth man to acquaintance; and, as the humble stream to the ocean, so doth it conduct him into the hard-acquired presence of the prince, whence fortune floweth.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Pleasure preconceived and preconcerted ends in disappointment; but disappointment, when it involves neither shame nor loss, is as good as success; for it supplies as many images to the mind, and as many topics to the tongue.
author: Johnson

text: We see but the outside of the rich man's happiness; few consider him to be like the silkworm, that, when she seems to play, is at the very same time spinning her own bowels and consuming herself.
author: Isaac Walton

text: Wherever you see a gaming-table, be very sure Fortune is not there.... She is ever seen accompanying industry, and as often trundling a wheelbarrow as lolling in a coach and six.
author: Goldsmith

text: Conscience does make cowards of us all; / And thus the native hue of resolution / Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought; / And enterprises of great pith and moment, / With this regard, their currents turn awry, / And lose the name of action.
author: Ham

text: If fortune would make a man estimable, she gives him virtues; if she would have him esteemed, she gives him success.
author: Joubert

text: Wild ambition loves to slide, not stand; / And Fortune's ice prefers to Virtue's land.
author: Dryden

text: Wisdom and Fortune combating together, / If that the former dare but what he can, / No chance may shake it.
author: Ant. and Cleo

text: To gather riches do not hazard health; / For, truth to say, health is the wealth of wealth.
author: Sir Richard Baker

text: Knowledge to their eyes her ample page, / Rich with the spoils of time, did ne'er unroll; / Chill penury repress'd their noble rage, / And froze the genial current of the soul.
author: Gray

text: We should manage our fortune like our constitution; enjoy it when good, have patience when bad, and never apply violent remedies but in cases of necessity.
author: La Roche

text: Very few people are good economists of their fortune, and still fewer of their time.
author: Chesterfield

text: Wise men, for the most part, are silent at present, and good men powerless; the senseless vociferate, and the heartless govern; while all social law and providence are dissolved by the enraged agitation of a multitude, among whom every villain has a chance of power, every simpleton of praise, and every scoundrel of fortune.
author: Ruskin

text: Duty scorns prudence, and criticism has few terrors for a man with a great purpose.
author: Disraeli

text: He who cannot profit you as a friend may at any time injure you as an enemy.
author: Gellert

text: War is a game which, were their subjects wise, kings should not play at.
author: Cowper

text: We should never so entirely avoid danger as to appear irresolute and cowardly; but, at the same time, we should avoid unnecessarily exposing ourselves to danger, than which nothing can be more foolish.
author: Cic

text: Knowledge is a perennial spring of wealth, ... and of itself is riches.
author: Saadi

text: Let no complaisance, no gentleness of temper, no weak desire of pleasing on your part, no wheedling, coaxing, nor flattery on other people's, make you recede one jot from any point that reason and prudence have bid you pursue.
author: Chesterfield

text: Philosophy, while it soothes the reason, damps the ambition.
author: Bulwer Lytton

text: I look upon an able statesman out of business like a huge whale, that will endeavour to overturn the ship unless he has an empty cask to play with.
author: Steele

text: Lose the habit of hard labour with its manliness, and then, / Comes the wreck of all you hope for in the wreck of noble men.
author: Dr. Walter Smith

text: So long as any Ideal (any soul of truth) does, in never so confused a manner, exist and work within the Actual, it is a tolerable business. Not so when the Ideal has wholly departed, and the Actual owns to no soul of truth any longer.
author: Carlyle

text: What the Puritans gave the world was not thought, but action.
author: Wendell Phillips

text: No belief of ours will change the facts or reverse the laws of the spiritual universe; and it is our first business to discover the laws and to learn how the facts stand.
author: Dr. Dale

text: Envy, among other ingredients, has a mixture of the love of justice in it. We are more angry at undeserved than at deserved good fortune.
author: Hazlitt

text: Wisdom is that attribute through which every action of a man receives its ideal value or import
author: Schleiermacher

text: Wisdom is a pearl; with most success / Sought in still water and beneath clear skies.
author: Cowper

text: Wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence: but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom giveth life to them that have it.
author: Bible

text: Seldom is a life wholly wrecked but the cause lies in some internal mal-arrangement, some want less of good fortune than of good guidance.
author: Carlyle

text: The way to wealth is as plain as the way to market; it depends chiefly on two words—industry and frugality.
author: Franklin

text: Wealth, power, and even the advantages of youth, have little to do with that which gives repose to the mind and firmness to the frame.
author: Scott

text: Youth is not rich in time; it may be, poor; part with it, as with money, sparing; pay no moment but in purchase of its worth; and what its worth ask death-beds, they can tell.
author: Young

text: Do not lose the present in vain perplexities about the future. If fortune lours to-day, she may smile to-morrow.
author: Sir T. Martin

text: Yet I've heard say, by wise men in my day, / That none are outwitted so easy as they / Who reckon with all men as if they suspect them, / And traffic in caution, and watch to detect them.
author: Dr. W. Smith

text: The wise man, even destitute of riches, enjoyeth elevated and very honourable stations; whilst the wretch, endowed with wealth, acquireth the post of disgrace.
author: Hitopadesa

text: The time of breeding is the time of doing children good; and not as many who think they have done fairly if they leave them a good portion after their decease.
author: George Herbert

text: Trusse up thy packe, and trudge from me, to every little boy, / And tell them thus from me, their time most happy is, / If to theyr time they reason had, to know the truth of this.
author: Chaucer

text: There is still a real magic in the action and reaction of minds on one another. The casual deliration of a few becomes, by this mysterious reverberation, the frenzy of many; men lose the use, not only of their understandings, but of their bodily senses; while the most obdurate unbelieving hearts melt like the rest in the furnace where all are cast as victims and as fuel.
author: Carlyle

text: Method will teach you to win time.
author: Goethe

text: Greatness is like a laced coat from Monmouth Street, which fortune lends us for a day to wear, to-morrow puts it on another's back.
author: Fielding

text: Genius is the very eye of intellect and the wing of thought; it is always in advance of its time, and is the pioneer for the generation which it precedes.
author: Simms

text: Full many a day for ever is lost / By delaying its work till to-morrow; / The minutes of sloth have often cost / Long years of bootless sorrow.
author: Eliza Cook

text: A mob is a body voluntarily bereaving itself of reason and traversing its work.
author: Emerson

text: Wit-work is always play, when it is good.
author: Ruskin

text: They that bear a noble mind, / Where they want of riches find.
author: Wither

text: A thrill passes through all men at the reception of a new truth, or at the performance of a great action, which comes out of the heart of nature.... By the necessity of our constitution, a certain enthusiasm attends the individual's consciousness of that Divine presence.
author: Emerson

text: Complaining profits little; stating of the truth may profit.
author: Carlyle

text: Half a man's wisdom goes with his courage.
author: Emerson

text: You must not think / That we are made of stuff so flat and dull, / That we can let our beard be shook with danger, / And think it pastime.
author: Ham

text: Whatever is new is unlooked for, and ever it mends some and impairs others; and he that is holpen takes it for a fortune, and he that is hurt for a wrong.
author: Bacon

text: Learning, like money, may be of so base a coin as to be utterly devoid of use; or, if sterling, may require good management to make it serve the purpose of sense and happiness.
author: Shenstone

text: Rich with the spoils of time.
author: Sir T. Browne

text: Genius of a kind is necessary to make a fortune, and especially a large one.
author: La Bruyère

text: Esteem is the harvest of a whole life spent in usefulness; but reputation is often bestowed upon a chance action, and depends most on success.
author: G. A. Sala

text: Skill to do comes of doing; knowledge comes by eyes always open, and working hands; and there is no knowledge that is not power.
author: Emerson

text: Think with awe on the slow, the quiet power of time.
author: Schiller

text: Thought is the seed of action; but action is as much its second form as thought is its first. It rises in thought, to the end that it may be uttered and acted. The more profound the thought, the more burdensome. Always in proportion to the depth of its sense does it knock importunately at the gates of the soul, to be spoken, to be done.
author: Emerson

text: But war's a game which, were their subjects wise, / Kings would not play at.
author: Cowper

text: We wrap ourselves up in the cloak of our own better fortune, and turn away our eyes, lest the wants and woes of our brother-mortals should disturb the selfish apathy of our souls.
author: Burns

text: Fortune favours the brave, as the old proverb says, but forethought much more.
author: Cic

text: If you dissemble sometimes your knowledge of that you are thought to know, you shall be thought, another time, to know that you know not.
author: Bacon

text: The bounds of a man's knowledge are easily concealed if he has but prudence.
author: Goldsmith

text: We take no note of time but from its loss.
author: Young

text: Unnumbered suppliants crowd preferment's gate, / Athirst for wealth, and burning to be great; / Delusive fortune hears the incessant call, / They mount, they shine, evaporate, and fall.
author: Johnson

text: Who shall say that Fortune grieves him, / While the star of hope she leaves him?
author: Burns

text: Reason has done, what it can do, when it discovers and draws up the law; to execute this law is reserved for him who feels the obligation of it, and has the due firmness of purpose.
author: Schiller

text: How are riches the means of happiness? In acquiring they create trouble, in their loss they occasion sorrow, and they are the cause of endless divisions amongst kindred!
author: Hitopadesa

text: The soul moralises the past in order not to be demoralised by it, and finds in the crucible of experience only the gold that she herself has poured into it.
author: Amiel

text: The conscious utterance of thought by speech or action, to any end, is art.
author: Emerson

text: Each man can learn something from his neighbour; at least he can learn to have patience with him—to live and let live.
author: Kingsley

text: Wealth heaped on wealth, nor truth nor safety buys; / The dangers gather as the treasures rise.
author: Johnson

text: Truth is the easiest part of all to play Present thyself as thou art and thou runnest no risk of falling out of thy rôle.
author: Rückert

text: Truth will be uppermost one time or another like cork, though kept down in the water.
author: Sir W. Temple

text: To the noble mind / Rich gifts wax poor when givers prove unkind.
author: Ham

text: The Stoic thought by slandering Happiness to woo her; by shunning to win her; and proudly presumed that, by fleeing her, she would turn and follow him.
author: Arliss

text: The fortune which nobody sees makes a man happy and unenvied.
author: Bacon

text: Thought, true labour of any kind, highest virtue itself, is it not the daughter of pain? Born as out of the black whirlwind; true effort in fact, as of a captive struggling to free itself—that is thought.
author: Carlyle

text: In misfortune, in error, and when the time appointed for certain affairs is about to elapse, a servant who hath his master's welfare at heart ought to speak unasked.
author: Hitopadesa

text: The person whose clothes are extremely fine I am too apt to consider as not being possessed of any superiority of fortune, but resembling those Indians who were found to wear all the gold they have in the world in a bob at the nose.
author: Goldsmith

text: Pure truth, like pure gold, has been found unfit for circulation, because men have discovered that it is far more convenient to adulterate the truth than to refine themselves. They will not advance their minds to the standard, therefore they lower the standard to their minds.
author: Colton

text: If it be asked, What is the improper expectation which it is dangerous to indulge, experience will quickly answer that it is such expectation as is dictated not by reason but by desire—an expectation that requires the common course of things to be changed, and the general rules of action to be broken.
author: Johnson

text: The wealth of both the Indies cannot redeem one single opportunity which you have once let slip.
author: Thomas à Kempis

text: The wisdom of life is in preventing all the evil we can, and using what is inevitable to the best purpose.
author: Ruskin

text: Where truth is not at the bottom, Nature will always be endeavouring to return, and will peep out and betray herself one time or other.
author: Tillotson

text: Fortune has rarely condescended to be the companion of genius.
author: Isaac Disraeli

text: Poverty palls the most generous spirits; it cows industry and casts resolution itself into despair.
author: Addison

text: None so wise but the advice of others may, at some time or other, be useful and necessary for him.
author: Thomas à Kempis

text: Most people think now-a-days the only hopeful way of serving your neighbour is to make a profit out of him; whereas, in my opinion, the hopefulest way of serving him is to let him make a profit out of me.
author: Ruskin

text: The world's wealth is its original men; by these and their works it is a world and not a waste; the memory and record of what Men it loves—this is the sum of its strength, its sacred "property for ever," whereby it upholds itself and steers forward, better or worse, through the yet undiscovered deep of Time.
author: Carlyle

text: Fortune is merry, and in this mood will give us anything.
author: Jul. Cæs

text: Prudence is that virtue by which we discern what is proper to be done under the various circumstances of time and place.
author: Milton

text: We do not know what is really good or bad fortune.
author: Rousseau

text: Bees will not work except in darkness; thought will not work except in silence; neither will virtue work except in secrecy.
author: Carlyle

text: Whether he be rich or whether he be poor, if he have a good heart, he shall at all times rejoice in a cheerful countenance; his mind shall tell him more than seven watchmen that sit above upon a tower on high.
author: Ecclus

text: It is we that are blind, not Fortune.
author: Sir T. Browne

text: Time is but the measure of the difficulty of a conception. Pure thought has scarcely any need of time, since it perceives the two ends of an idea almost the same moment.
author: Amiel

text: Happy is the man who can endure the highest and the lowest fortune. He who has endured such vicissitudes with equanimity has deprived misfortune of its power.
author: Sen

text: Invention is the talent of youth, and judgment of age.
author: Swift

text: Wealth is a shift. The wise man angles with himself only, and with no meaner bait.
author: Emerson

text: Wisdom is intrinsically of a silent nature; it cannot at once, or completely at all, be read off in words, and is only legible in whole when its work is done.
author: Carlyle

text: Want of prudence is too frequently the want of virtue; nor is there on earth a more powerful advocate for vice than poverty.
author: Goldsmith

text: The essence of true nobility is neglect of self. Let the thought of self pass in, and the beauty of a great action is gone, like the bloom from a soiled flower.
author: Froude

text: Mysteries which must explain themselves are not worth the loss of time which a conjecture about them takes up.
author: Sterne

text: Think of ease, but work on.
author: George Herbert

text: Fortune is not content to do a man one ill turn.
author: Bacon

text: The best work never was, nor ever will be, done for money at all.
author: Ruskin

text: Every genuine work of art has as much reason for being as the earth and the sun.
author: Emerson

text: Truth should be strenuous and bold; but the strongest things are not always the noisiest, as any one may see who compares scolding with logic.
author: Chapin

text: Genius is the gold in the mine; talent is the miner who works and brings it out.
author: Lady Blessington

text: The less we deserve good fortune, the more we hope for it.
author: Molière

text: The honest heart that's free frae a' / Intended fraud or guile, / However Fortune kick the ba', / Has aye some cause to smile.
author: Burns

text: Difficulties strengthen the mind, as labour does the body.
author: Sen

text: Lamenting becomes fools, and action wise folk.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: The greatest of all economists are the fortifying virtues, which the wisest men of all time have arranged under the general heads of Prudence, or Discretion, the spirit which discerns and adopts rightly; Justice, the spirit which rules and divides rightly; Fortitude, the spirit which persists and endures rightly; and Temperance, the spirit which stops and refuses rightly.
author: Ruskin

text: I believe there are few persons who, if they please to reflect on their past lives, will not find that had they saved all those little sums which they have spent unnecessarily they might at present have been masters of a competent fortune.
author: Eustace Budgell

text: Read not books alone, but men, and amongst them chiefly thyself; if thou find anything questionable there, use the commentary of a severe friend rather than the gloss of a sweet-lipped flatterer; there is more profit in a distasteful truth than deceitful sweetness.
author: Quarles

text: Rich men without wisdom and learning are but sheep with golden fleeces.
author: Solon

text: When a youth is fully in love with a girl, and feels that he is wise in loving her, he should at once tell her so plainly, and take his chance bravely with other suitors.
author: Ruskin

text: Sacred courage indicates that a man loves an idea better than all things in the world; that he is aiming neither at self nor comfort, but will venture all to put in act the invisible thought in his mind.
author: Emerson

text: The most part of all the misery and mischief, of all that is denominated evil, in the world, arises from the face that men are too remiss to get a proper knowledge of their aims, and when they do know them, to work intensely in attaining them.
author: Goethe

text: What was my morning's thought, at night's the same; / The poor and rich but differ in the name. / Content's the greatest bliss we can procure / Frae 'boon the lift; without it kings are poor.
author: Allan Ramsay

text: Words are wise men's counters, but they are the money of fools.
author: Hobbes

text: In the dullest existence there is a sheen of inspiration or of madness (thou partly hast it in thy choice which of the two) that gleams in from the circumambient eternity, and colours with its own hues our little islet of time.
author: Carlyle

text: He that will carry nothing about him but gold will be every day at a loss for readier change.
author: Pope

text: Can wealth give happiness? look around and see, / What gay distress! what splendid misery! / Whatever fortunes lavishly can pour, / The mind annihilates and calls for more.
author: Young

text: Let this be an example for the acquisition of all knowledge, virtue, and riches. By the fall of drops of water, by degrees, a pot is filled.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Wise sayings are the guiding oracles which man has found out for himself in that great business of ours, of learning how to be, to do, to do without, and to depart.
author: John Morley

text: Persons of fine manners make behaviour the first sign of force,—behaviour, and not performance, or talent, or, much less, wealth.
author: Emerson

text: Heroism is the brilliant triumph of the soul over fear; fear of poverty, of suffering, of calumny, of sickness, of isolation and death.... It is the dazzling and glorious concentration of courage.
author: Amiel

text: Letters of mere compliment, congratulation, or affected condolence, which have cost the authors most labour in composing, never fail of being the most disagreeable and insipid to the readers.
author: Blair

text: To catch dame Fortune's golden smile, / Assiduous wait upon her; / And gather gear by ev'ry wile / That's justified by honour; / Not for to hide it in a hedge, / Nor for a train attendant, / But for the glorious privilege / Of being independent.
author: Burns

text: To seize a character, even that of one man, in its life and secret mechanism, requires a philosopher; to delineate it with truth and impressiveness, is work for a poet.
author: Carlyle

text: The rich are always advising the poor; but the poor seldom venture to return the compliment.
author: Helps

text: Riches do not exhilarate us so much by their possession as they torment us with their loss.
author: Gregory

text: He who has not known poverty, sorrow, contradiction, and the rest, and learned from them the priceless lessons they have to teach, has missed a good opportunity of schooling.
author: Carlyle

text: Chance will not do the work: / Chance sends the breeze, / But if the pilot slumber at the helm, / The very wind that wafts us towards the port / May dash us on the shelves.
author: Scott

text: Knowledge produceth humility; from humility proceedeth worthiness; from worthiness riches are acquired; from riches religion, and thence happiness.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Skill is the united force of experience, intellect and passion in their operation on manual labour.
author: Ruskin

text: It is more honourable to be raised to a throne than be born to one; fortune bestows the one, merit obtains the other.
author: Petrarch

text: Poverty, incessant drudgery, and much worse evils, it has often been the lot of poets and wise men to strive with, and their glory to conquer.
author: Carlyle

text: When affliction thunders over our roofs, to hide our heads and run into our graves shows us no men, but makes us fortune's slaves.
author: Ben Jonson

text: We must labour unceasingly to render our piety reasonable, and our reason pious.
author: Mme. Swetchine

text: We need greater virtues to sustain good than evil fortune.
author: La Roche

text: Commerce is one of the daughters of Fortune, inconstant and deceitful as her mother. She chooses her residence where she is least expected, and shifts her abode when her continuance is, in appearance, most firmly settled.
author: Johnson

text: Fortune reigns in the gifts of the world, not in the lineaments of nature.
author: As You Like It

text: The true labourer is worthy of his hire, but, in the beginning and first choice of industry, his heart must not be the heart of an hireling.
author: Ruskin

text: Our better mind / Is as a Sunday's garment, then put on / When we have nought to do; but at our work / We wear a worse for thrift.
author: Crowe

text: When a thought of Plato becomes a thought to me,—when a truth that fired the soul of Pindar fires mine, time is no more.
author: Emerson

text: What the universe was thought to be in Judea and other places, this may be very interesting to know; what it is in England here where we live and have our work to do, that is the interesting point.
author: Carlyle

text: Man is not born to be free, and for the noble there is no fairer fortune than to serve a prince whom he honours.
author: Goethe

text: If happiness ha'e not her seat / And centre in the breast, / We may be wise, or rich, or great, / But never can be blest.
author: Burns

text: Work, go, fall, rise, speak, be silent! In this manner do the rich sport with those needy men, who are held by the grip of dependence.
author: Hitopadesa

text: To eat or drink too much, to play too much, to work too much, or to grumble too much—all these are equally pernicious.
author: John Wagstaffe

text: It requires a great deal of boldness and a great deal of caution to make a great fortune, and when you have got it, it requires ten times as much wit to keep it.
author: Emerson

text: Never yet has it been our fortune to fall in with any man of genius whose conclusions did not correspond better with his premises, and not worse, than those of other men; whose genius, once understood, did not manifest itself in a deeper, fuller, truer view of all things human and divine, than the clearest of your so-called laudable "practical men" had claim to.
author: Carlyle

text: Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both?
author: Ecclus

text: Truth reaches her full action by degrees, and not at once.
author: Draper

text: The real science of political economy is that which teaches nations to desire and labour for the things that lead to life; and which teaches them to scorn and destroy the things that lead to destruction.
author: Ruskin

text: Many speak the truth when they say that they despise riches and preferment; but they mean the riches and preferment possessed by other men.
author: Colton

text: How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!
author: Bible

text: Detraction's a bold monster, and fears not / To wound the fame of princes, if it find / But any blemish in their lives to work on.
author: Massinger

text: Nothing recommends a man more to the female mind than courage.
author: Spectator

text: Life was never a May-game for men; not play at all, but hard work, that makes the sinews sore and the heart sore.
author: Carlyle

text: Conversation is a traffic; and if you enter into it without some stock of knowledge to balance the account perpetually, the trade drops at once.
author: Sterne

text: There are but two ways of paying debt—increase of industry in raising income; increase of thrift in laying it out.
author: Carlyle

text: Smile (Fortune), and we smile, the lords of many lands; / Frown, and we smile, the lords of our own hands; / For man is man and master of his fate.
author: Tennyson

text: It is the great error of reformers and philanthropists in our time to nibble at the consequences of unjust power, instead of redressing the injustice itself.
author: J. S. Mill

text: The reason why so few marriages are happy is because young ladies spend their time in making nets, not in making cages.
author: Swift

text: There is nothing really more monstrous in any recorded savagery or absurdity of mankind than that governments should be able to get money for any folly they choose to commit, by selling to capitalists the right of taxing future generations to the end of time.
author: Ruskin

text: Let any man compare his present fortune with the past, and he will probably find himself, upon the whole, neither better nor worse than formerly.
author: Goldsmith

text: Truth is never learned, in any department of industry, by arguing, but by working and observing.
author: Ruskin

text: The price of wisdom is above rubies.
author: Bible

text: A man who cannot mind his own business is not to be trusted with the king's.
author: Saville

text: Flattery's the turnpike road to Fortune's door.
author: Walcot

text: A wise man should have money in his head, but not in his heart.
author: Swift

text: Let not one look of fortune cast you down; / She were not fortune if she did not frown; / Such as do braveliest bear her scorns awhile / Are those on whom at last she most will smile.
author: Orrery

text: Why complain of wanting light? It is courage, energy, perseverance that I want.
author: Carlyle

text: Fortune is like a mirror—it does not alter men; it only shows men just as they are.
author: Billings

text: That is a most wretched fortune which is without an enemy.
author: Pub. Syr

text: Were wisdom to be sold, she would give no price; every man is satisfied with the share he has from nature.
author: Henry Home

text: Reverence the highest, have patience with the lowest. Let this day's performance of the meanest duty be thy religion. Are the stars too distant, pick up the pebble that lies at thy feet and from it learn the all.
author: Margaret Fuller

text: Farewell the tranquil mind! farewell content! / Farewell the plumed troop and the big wars / That make ambition virtue! oh, farewell! / Farewell the neighing steed and the shrill trump, / The spirit-stirring drum, the ear-piercing fife, / The royal banner, and all quality, / Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war!
author: Othello

text: Patience, and shuffle the cards.
author: Cervantes

text: The sweetest music is not in the oratorio, but in the human voice when it speaks from its instant life tones of tenderness, truth, or courage.
author: Emerson

text: Fortune is like the market, where many times, if you can stay a little, the price will fall.
author: Bacon

text: The most sorrowful occurrence often, through the hand of Providence, takes the most favourable turn for our happiness; the succession of fortune and misfortune in life is intertwined like sleep and waking, neither without the other, and one for the sake of the other.
author: Goethe

text: We should round every day of stirring action with an evening of thought. We learn nothing of our experience except we muse upon it.
author: Bovee

text: The essence of greatness is the perception that virtue is enough. Poverty is its ornament. It does not need plenty, and can very well abide its loss.
author: Emerson

text: The greatest events of an age are its best thoughts. It is the nature of thought to find its way into action.
author: Bovee

text: Seldom ever was any knowledge given to keep but to impart; the grace of this rich jewel is lost in concealment.
author: Bp. Hall

text: Time gives prudence; the lord of time, inspiration; the one is a reward, the other a gift.
author: Börne

text: Knowledge conquered by labour becomes a possession—a property entirely our own.
author: S. Smiles

text: To strive to get rid of an evil is to aim at something definite, but to desire a better fortune than we have is blind folly.
author: Goethe

text: Whatever the benefits of fortune are, they yet require a palate fit to relish and taste them; it is fruition, and not possession, that renders us happy.
author: Montaigne

text: Every man is the architect of his own fortune.
author: Sallust

text: The phœnix, Hope, can wing her flight / Through the vast deserts of the skies, / And still defying fortune's spite, / Revive and from her ashes rise.
author: Cervantes

text: He is wise who can instruct us and assist us in the business of daily virtuous living; he who trains us to see old truth under academic formularies may be wise or not, as it chances, but we love to see wisdom in unpretending forms, to recognise her royal features under a week-day vesture.
author: Carlyle

text: Work earnestly at anything, you will by degrees learn to work at almost all things.
author: Carlyle

text: The wise man should study the acquisition of science and riches as if he were not subject to sickness and death; but to the duties of religion he should attend as if death had seized him by the hair.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Friendship is too pure a pleasure for a mind cankered with ambition or the lust of power and grandeur.
author: Junius

text: Gambling with cards, or dice, or stocks, is all one thing; it is getting money without giving an equivalent for it.
author: Ward Beecher

text: Ignorance is bold, and knowledge reserved.
author: Thucydides

text: Wealth leaves us at death; kinsmen at the grave; but virtues of the mind unto the heavens with us we have.
author: Lord Vaux

text: The wisdom of nations lies in their proverbs, which are brief and pithy. Collect and learn them; they are notable measures and directions for human life; you have much in little; they save time in speaking; and upon occasion may be the fullest and safest answers.
author: William Penn

text: The soldier's trade, verily and essentially, is not slaying, but being slain ... and the reason the world honours the soldier is because he holds his life at the service of the state.
author: Ruskin

text: Truth is simple indeed, but we have generally no small trouble in learning to apply it to any practical purpose.
author: Goethe

text: Whoever aims at doing or enjoying all and everything with his entire nature, whoever tries to link together all that is without him by such a species of enjoyment will only lose his time in efforts that can never be successful.
author: Goethe

text: The world is a thing that man must learn to despise, and even to neglect, before he can learn to reverence it, and work in it and for it.
author: Carlyle

text: To the minnow every cranny and pebble, and quality and accident, of its little native creek may have become familiar; but does the minnow understand the ocean tides and periodic currents, the trade-winds, and monsoons, and moon's eclipses; by all of which the condition of its little creek is regulated, and may (from time to time, unmiraculously enough) be quite overset and reversed? Such a minnow is man; his creek, this planet earth; his ocean, the immeasurable All; his monsoons and periodic currents, the mysterious course of Providence through æons of æons.
author: Carlyle

text: We do not commonly find men of superior sense amongst those of the highest fortune.
author: Juv

text: Laws are not our life, only the house wherein our life is led; nay, they are but the bare walls of the house; all whose essential furniture, the inventions and traditions and daily habits that regulate and support our existence, are the work not of Dracos and Hampdens, but of Phœnician mariners, of Italian masons, and Saxon metallurgists, of philosophers, alchymists, prophets, and the long-forgotten train of artists and artisans, who from the first have been jointly teaching us how to think and how to act, how to rule over spiritual and physical nature.
author: Carlyle

text: We unconsciously imitate what pleases us, and insensibly approximate to the characters we most admire. In this way, a generous habit of thought and of action carries with it an incalculable influence.
author: Bovee

text: Truth, like the sun, submits to be obscured; but, like the sun, only for a time.
author: Bovee

text: He is a great man who inhabits a higher sphere of thought, into which other men rise with labour and difficulty: he has but to open his eyes to see things in a true light and in large relations, while they must make painful corrections, and keep a vigilant eye on many sources of error.
author: Emerson

text: Wise men ne'er sit and wail their loss, / But cheerly seek how to redress their harms.
author: Hen. VI

text: When, in your last hour (think of this), all faculty in the broken spirit shall fade away and sink into inanity—imagination, thought, effort, enjoyment—then will the flower of belief, which blossoms even in the night, remain to refresh you with its fragrance in the last darkness.
author: Jean Paul

text: Twenty people can gain money for one who can use it; and the vital question for individuals and for nations, is never "how much do they make," but "to what purpose do they spend."
author: Ruskin

text: Learn to labour and to wait.
author: Longfellow

text: The chief of all the curses of this unhappy age is the universal gabble of its fools, and of the flocks that follow them, rendering the quiet voices of the wise of all past time inaudible.
author: Ruskin

text: Let us, then, be up and doing, / With a heart for every fate; / Still achieving, still pursuing, / Learn to labour and to wait.
author: Longfellow

text: Knowledge is the consequence of time, and multitude of days are fittest to teach wisdom.
author: Jeremy Collier

text: The disputes of two of equal strength and fortune are worthy of attention; but not of two, the one great, the other humble.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Success (by laws of competition) signifies always so much victory over your neighbour as to obtain the direction of his work and take the profits of it. This is the real source of all great riches.
author: Ruskin

text: A fool may sometimes have talent, but he never has judgment.
author: La Roche

text: How rarely reason guides the stubborn choice, / Rules the bold hand or prompts the suppliant voice.
author: Johnson

text: She pined in thought, / And with a green and yellow melancholy. / She sat like patience on a monument, / Smiling at grief.
author: Twelfth Night

text: No man can become largely rich by his personal toil, but only by discovery of some method of taxing the labour of others.
author: Ruskin

text: Fortune makes him a fool whom she makes her darling.
author: Bacon

text: Good unexpected, evil unforeseen, / Appear by turns, as fortune shifts the scene; / Some rais'd aloft, come tumbling down amain / And fall so hard, they bound and rise again.
author: Lord Lansdowne

text: Wise sayings are not only for ornament, but for action and business, having a point or edge, whereby knots in business are pierced and discovered.
author: Bacon

text: Happy men are full of the present, for its bounty suffices them; and wise men also, for its duties engage them. Our grand business undoubtedly is not to see what lies dimly at a distance, but to do what lies clearly at hand.
author: Carlyle

text: If one were to think constantly of death, the business of life would stand still.
author: Johnson

text: Ordinary people think merely of spending time; a man with any brains, of using it.
author: Schopenhauer

text: The merchant who was at first busy in acquiring money ceases to grow richer from the time when he makes it his business only to count it.
author: Johnson

text: Ovid finely compares a man of broken fortune to a falling column; the lower it sinks, the greater weight it is obliged to sustain.
author: Goldsmith

text: Work is of a religious nature,—work is of a brave nature, which it is the aim of all religion to be. "All work of man is as the swimmer's." By incessant wise defiance of it, lusty rebuke and buffet of it, behold how it loyally supports him,—bears him as its conqueror along! "It is so," says Goethe, "with all things that man undertakes in this world."
author: Carlyle

text: Sorrows are often evolved from good fortune.
author: Goethe

text: Gross and vulgar minds will always pay a higher respect to wealth than to talent; for wealth, although it is a far less efficient source of power than talent, happens to be far more intelligible.
author: Colton

text: A wise physician, skill'd our wounds to heal, / Is more than armies to the public weal.
author: Pope

text: Labour of the hands, even when pursued to the verge of drudgery, is perhaps never the worst form of idleness (for the mind); it has a constant and imperishable moral.
author: Thoreau

text: Music fills up the present moment more decisively than anything else, whether it awakens thought or summons to action.
author: Goethe

text: There is a tide in the affairs of men, / Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; / Omitted, all the voyage of their life / Is bound in shallows and in miseries; / On such a full sea are we now afloat; / And we must take the current when it serves, / Or lose our ventures.
author: Jul. Cæs

text: Hitherto doth love on fortune tend; / For who not needs, shall never lack a friend; / And who in want a hollow friend doth try, / Directly seasons him his enemy.
author: Ham

text: Man's true, genuine estimate, / The grand criterion of his fate, / Is not—Art thou high or low? / Did thy fortune ebb or flow?

text: How happy is he born or taught / That serveth not another's will; / Whose armour is his honest thought, / And simple truth his utmost skill.
author: Sir Henry Wotton

text: That which is past is gone and irrevocable, and wise men have enough to do with things present and to come; therefore they do but trifle with themselves that labour in past matters.
author: Bacon

text: They are not a pipe for fortune's finger, / To sound what stop she please.
author: Ham

text: It is only by labour that thought can be made healthy, and only by thought that labour can be made happy.
author: Ruskin

text: "Truth," I cried, "though the heavens crush me for following her; no falsehood, though a whole celestial Lubberland were the price of apostasy!"

text: Fortune brings in some boats that are ill-steered.
author: Cymbeline

text: Peacefully and reasonably to contemplate is at no time hurtful, and while we use ourselves to think of the advantages of others, our own mind comes insensibly to imitate them; and every false activity to which our fancy was alluring us is then willingly abandoned.

text: Truth is to be costly to you—of labour and patience; and you are never to sell it, but to guard and to give.

text: Children think not of what is past, nor what is to come, but enjoy the present time, which few of us do.

text: If fortune favour you, be not elated; if she frown, do not despond.

text: Faith is not reason's labour, but repose.
author: Young

text: Fight on, thou brave true heart, and falter not, through dark fortune and through bright, the cause thou fightest for, so far as it is true, is very sure of victory.

text: There are no obstructions more fatal to fortune than pride and resentment.

text: The wise men of old have sent most of their morality down the stream of time in the light skiff of apothegm or epigram.

text: He who conforms to the rule which the genius of the human understanding whispers secretly in the ear of every new-born being, viz., to test action by thought and thought by action, cannot err; and if he errs, he will soon find himself again in the right way.

text: Gentlemen have to learn that it is no part of their duty or privilege to live on other people's toil; that there is no degradation in the hardest manual or the humblest servile labour, when it is honest.

text: To guard from error is not the instructor's business; but to lead the erring pupil.
author: Goethe

text: Remember, now, when you meet your antagonist, to do everything in a mild agreeable manner. Let your courage be keen, but, at the same time, as polished as your sword.

text: The man who will live above his present circumstances is in great danger of living in a little time much beneath them, or, as the Italian proverb says, "The man who lives by hope will die by despair."
author: Addison

text: Talent, lying in the understanding, is often inherited; genius, being the action of reason and imagination, rarely or never.
author: Coleridge

text: If ill thoughts at any time enter into the mind of a good man, he doth not roll them under his tongue as a sweet morsel.
author: Matthew Henry

text: The bell strikes one. We take no note of time / But for its loss.
author: Young

text: Unbounded courage and compassion join'd, / Tempting each other in the victor's mind, / Alternately proclaim him good and great, / And make the hero and the man complete.

text: It is better to live in a haunted forest ... than to live amongst relations after the loss of wealth.

text: Greatness, once fallen out with fortune, / Must fall out with men too; what the declined is, / He shall as soon read in the eyes of others / As feel in his own fall.

text: The civilised nation consists broadly of mob, money-collecting machine, and capitalist; and when the mob wishes to spend money for any purpose, it sets its money-collecting machine to borrow the money it needs from the capitalist, who lends it on condition of taxing the mob generation after generation.
author: Ruskin

text: The great error of our nature is, not to know where to stop, not to be satisfied with any reasonable acquirement, not to compound with our condition; but to lose all we have gained by an insatiable pursuit after more.

text: It is difficult to act a part long, for where truth is not at the bottom, nature will peep out and betray itself one time or other.
author: South

text: Virtue, like a strong and hardy plant, will root when it can find an ingenuous nature and a mind not averse to labour.
author: Plutarch

text: Nature listening stood whilst Shakespeare play'd, / And wonder'd at the work herself had made.
author: Churchill

text: Most men of action incline to fatalism, and most men of thought believe in Providence.
author: Balzac

text: Money is a bottomless sea, in which honour, conscience, and truth may be drowned.
author: Kazlay

text: Judgment is not a swift-growing plant; it requires time and culture to mature it.
author: H. Ballou

text: Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established; and by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches.
author: Bible

text: We always take credit for the good, and attribute the bad to fortune.
author: La Fontaine

text: Ne'er grudge and carp, / Though fortune use you hard and sharp.
author: Burns

text: Time destroys the speculations of man, but it confirms the judgment of nature.
author: Cic

text: Good fortune is the offspring of our endeavours, although there be nothing sweeter than ease.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Go, wondrous creature, mount where science guides. / Go, measure earth, weigh air, and state the tides; / Instruct the planets in what orbs to run, / Correct old Time, and regulate the sun; / Go, teach Eternal Wisdom how to rule, / Then drop into thyself and be a fool.
author: Pope

text: L'esclave n'a qu'un maître; l'ambitieux en a autant qu'il y a de gens utiles à sa fortune
author: La Bruyère

text: No man can read with profit that which he cannot learn to read with pleasure.
author: Noah Porter

text: Who can compute what the world loses in the multitude of promising intellects combined with timid characters, who dare not follow out any bold, vigorous, independent train of thought, lest it should land them in something which would admit of being considered irreligious or immoral?
author: J. S. Mill

text: The question is not at what door of fortune's palace shall we enter in, but what doors does she open to us?
author: Burns

text: Union does everything when it is perfect; it satisfies desires, it simplifies needs, it foresees the wishes of the imagination; it is an aisle always open, and becomes a constant fortune.
author: De Senancour

text: Think'st thou existence doth depend on time? / It doth; but actions are our epochs.
author: Byron

text: Each good thought or action moves / The dark world nearer to the sun.
author: Whittier

text: Truth is simple and gives little trouble, but falsehood gives occasion for the frittering away of time and strength.
author: Goethe

text: Would we but pledge ourselves to truth as heartily as we do to a real or imaginary mistress, and think life too short only because it abridges our time of service, what a new world we should have!
author: Lowell

text: Knowledge is not an inert and passive principle, which comes to us whether we will or no; but it must be sought before it can be won; it is the product of great labour, and therefore of great sacrifice.
author: Buckle

text: Diligence is the mother of good fortune.
author: Cervantes

text: There is no greater wisdom than well to time the beginnings and onset of things.
author: Bacon

text: The end of man is an action, not a thought, though it were the noblest.
author: Carlyle

text: To simplify complications is, in all branches of knowledge, the first essential of success.
author: Buckle

text: To be bodily tranquil, to speak little, and to digest without effort are absolutely necessary to grandeur of mind or of presence, or to proper development of genius.
author: Balzac

text: Providence has decreed that those common acquisitions—money, gems, plate, noble mansions, and dominion—should be sometimes bestowed on the indolent and unworthy; but those things which constitute our true riches, and which are properly our own, must be procured by our own labour.
author: Erasmus

text: Every great mind seeks to labour for eternity. All men are captivated by immediate advantages; great minds alone are excited by the prospect of distant good.
author: Schiller

text: Has any man, or any society of men, a truth to speak, a piece of spiritual work to do; they can nowise proceed at once and with the mere natural organs, but must first call a public meeting, appoint committees, issue prospectuses, eat a public dinner; in a word, construct or borrow machinery, wherewith to speak it and do it. Without machinery they were hopeless, helpless; a colony of Hindoo weavers squatting in the heart of Lancashire.
author: Carlyle

text: Slight not the smallest loss, whether it be / In love or honour; take account of all: / Shine like the sun in every corner: see / Whether thy stock of credit swell or fall.
author: George Herbert

text: When a man becomes dear to me, I have touched the goal of fortune.
author: Emerson

text: Eccentricity has always abounded when and where strength of character has abounded; and the amount of eccentricity in a society has been proportional to the amount of genius, mental vigour, and moral courage it contained. That so few now dare to be eccentric, marks the chief danger of the time.
author: J. S. Mill

text: Knowledge is like current coin. A man may have some right to be proud of possessing it, (only) if he has worked for the gold of it, and assayed it, and stamped it, so that it may be received of all men as true, or earned it fairly, being already assayed.
author: Ruskin

text: The tallest trees are most in the power of the winds, and ambitious men of the blasts of fortune.
author: Wm. Penn

text: If new-got gold is said to burn the pockets till it be cast forth into circulation, much more may new truth.
author: Carlyle

text: We must, if we would husband life and not waste it, bravely resolve to dispense with the dispensable, to content ourselves with the minimum of want, to stake our reputation, if such be dear to us, upon intrinsic worth, and show once again, if we can, by our mere life and labour, what are the "roots of honour" and the "veins of wealth."
author: Ed

text: Sin seen from the thought is a diminution or loss; seen from the conscience or will, it is a pravity or bad.
author: Emerson

text: On the pinnacle of fortune man does not stand long firm.
author: Goethe

text: Love is not to be reason'd down or lost / In high ambition or a thirst of greatness.
author: Addison

text: If fortune give thee less than she has done, / Then make less fire, and walk more in the sun.
author: Sir R. Baker

text: We, ignorant of ourselves, / Beg often our own harms, which the wise powers / Deny us for our good; so find we profit / By losing of our prayers.
author: Ant. and Cleo

text: Learn to be pleased with everything; with wealth so far as it makes us of benefit to others; with poverty, for not having much to care for; and with obscurity, for being unenvied.
author: Plutarch

text: Emotion turning back on itself, and not leading on to thought or action, is the element of madness.
author: John Sterling

text: The courage of truth is the first condition of philosophic study.
author: Hegel

text: Deliberate with caution, but act with decision; and yield with graciousness or oppose with firmness.
author: Colton

text: Man must serve his time to every trade / Save censure; critics all are ready made.
author: Byron

text: Whatever bit of a wise man's work is honestly and benevolently done, that bit is his book or his piece of art.
author: Ruskin

text: Perseverance and audacity generally win.
author: Mme. Deluzy

text: Great men should think of opportunity, and not of time. Time is the excuse of feeble and puzzled spirits.
author: Disraeli

text: It is madness to make fortune the mistress of events, because in herself she is nothing, but is ruled by prudence.
author: Dryden

text: The way of the superior man is threefold—virtuous, he is free from anxieties; wise, he is free from perplexities; bold, he is free from fear.
author: Confucius

text: Better to get wisdom than gold.
author: Bible

text: Fling away ambition; / By that sin fell the angels; how can man, then, / The image of his Maker, hope to win by it?
author: Hen. VIII

text: Nothing is a misery, / Unless our weakness apprehend it so; / We cannot be more faithful to ourselves / In anything that's manly, than to make / Ill-fortune as contemptible to us / As it makes us to others.
author: Beaumont and Fletcher

text: What, though thou wert rich and of high esteem, dost thou yield to sorrow because of thy loss of fortune?
author: Hitopadesa

text: Happy in that we are not over-happy; / On Fortune's cap we are not the very button.
author: Ham

text: The desire of power in excess caused the angels to fall; the desire of knowledge in excess caused man to fall; but in charity there is no excess, neither can man or angel come in danger by it.
author: Bacon

text: Friends and acquaintances are the surest passports to fortune.
author: Schopenhauer

text: We should guard against a talent which we cannot hope to practise in perfection. Improve it as we may, we shall always in the end, when the merit of the master has become apparent to us, painfully lament the loss of time and strength devoted to such botching.
author: Goethe

text: The wise weigh their words in a balance for gold.
author: Ecclus

text: We inherit, not life only, but all the garniture and form of life; and work, and speak, and even think and feel, as our fathers, and primeval grandfathers, from the beginning, have given it us.
author: Carlyle

text: His own character is the arbiter of every one's fortune.
author: Pub. Syr

text: Happiness springs not from a large fortune, but temperate habits and simple wishes. Riches increase not by increase of the supply of want, but by decrease of the sense of it,—the minimum of it being the maximum of them.
author: Ed

text: Hoist up the sail while gale doth last—/ Tide and wind wait no man's pleasure! / Seek not time when time is past—/ Sober speed is wisdom's leisure!
author: Southwell

text: Let fortune empty her whole quiver on me, / I have a soul that, like an ample shield, / Can take in all, and verge enough for more.
author: Dryden

text: Folks as have no mind to be o' use have always the luck to be out o' the road when there's anything to be done.
author: George Eliot

text: Our stomach for good fortune is bottomless, but the entrance to it is narrow.
author: Schopenhauer

text: When Fortune means to men most good, / She looks upon them with a threatening eye.
author: King John

text: Free will I be in thought and in poetry; in action the world hampers us enough.
author: Goethe

text: For truth is precious and divine, / Too rich a pearl for carnal swine.

author: Goldsmith

author: Ben Jonson

text: Many people take no care of their money till they have come nearly to an end of it, and others do just the same with their time.

author: Johnson

text: Tired Nature's sweet restorer, balmy Sleep! / He, like the world, his ready visit pays / Where Fortune smiles; the wretched he forsakes: / Swift on his downy pinions flies from woe, / And lights on lids unsullied with a tear.

text: Love to make others happy; yes, surely at all times, so far as you can. But at bottom that is not the aim of any life. Do not think that your life means a mere searching in gutters for fallen creatures to wipe and set up.... In our life there is no meaning at all except the work we have done.

text: Action is but coarsened thought.

author: Carlyle

text: Men still are what they always have been, a medley of strength and weakness, often obedient to reason, and oftener to passion; so have they come down the stream of time for six thousand years, and mostly in such shape as the moment has fashioned them.

text: Fortune! There is no fortune; all is trial, or punishment, or recompense, or foresight.

text: Freedom is a new religion—the religion of our time.
author: Heine

text: True fortitude I take to be the quiet possession of a man's self, and an undisturbed doing his duty, whatever evil besets him or danger lies in his way.
author: Locke

text: Wit and wisdom are born with a man.
author: Selden

text: Every generous action loves the public view, yet no theatre for virtue is equal to a consciousness of it.
author: Cic

text: He that lacks time to mourn lacks time to mend.
author: Sir H. Taylor

text: Gain at the expense of reputation should be called loss.
author: Pub. Syr

text: It is delightful, after wandering in the thick darkness of metaphysics, to behold again the fair face of Truth.
author: Carlyle

text: Use makes a better soldier than the most urgent considerations of duty—familiarity with danger enabling him to estimate the danger. He sees how much is the risk, and is not afflicted with imagination; knows practically Marshal Saxe's rule, that every soldier killed costs the enemy his weight in lead.
author: Emerson

text: You may know a wise man by his election of an aim, and a sagacious by his election of the means.
author: Rückert

text: Strength of mind is exercise, not rest.
author: Pope

text: I will be as harsh as truth and as uncompromising as justice.
author: W. Lloyd Garrison

text: Nature transcends all our moods of thought, and its secret we do not yet find.
author: Emerson

text: Only truth can be polished.
author: Ruskin

text: Let him who would move and convince others be first moved and convinced himself. author: Carlyle

text: The happiness of man depends on no creed and no book; it depends on the dominion of truth, which is the redeemer and saviour, the Messiah and the King of glory.
author: Rabbi Wise

text: Reason requires culture to expand it. It resembles the fire concealed in the flint, which only shows itself when struck with the steel.
author: Gordil

text: Fell luxury! more perilous to youth than storms or quicksands, poverty or chains.
author: Hannah More

text: In books lies the soul of the whole past time; the articulate audible voice of the past, when the body and material substance of it has altogether vanished like a dream.
author: Carlyle

text: Work is the mission of man on this planet.
author: Carlyle

text: No statesman e'er will find it worth his pains / To tax our labours and excise our brains.
author: Churchill

text: Art is the path of the creator to his work.
author: Emerson

text: Persons are love's world, and the coldest philosopher cannot recount the debt of the young soul, wandering here in nature to the power of love, without being tempted to unsay, as treasonable to nature, aught derogatory to the social instincts.
author: Emerson

text: To talk without effort is, after all, the great charm of talking.
author: Hare

text: Few things are more unpleasant than the transaction of business with men who are above knowing or caring what they have to do.
author: Johnson

text: For he that worketh high and wise, / Nor pauses in his plan, / Will take the sun out of the skies / Ere freedom out of man.
author: Emerson

text: No earnest thinker is a plagiarist pure and simple. He will never borrow from others that which he has not already, more or less, thought out for himself.
author: C. Kingsley

text: Three poets in three distant ages born, / Greece, Italy, and England did adorn. / The first in loftiness of thought surpass'd; / The next, in majesty; in both, the last. / The force of Nature could no further go; / To make a third, she join'd the former two.
author: Dryden

text: Find earth where grows no weed, and you may find a heart where no error grows.
author: Knowles

text: Human nature ... / Is not a punctual presence, but a spirit / Diffused through time and space.
author: Wordsworth

text: Know then this truth (enough for man to know), / Virtue alone is happiness below.
author: Pope

text: Error, sterile in itself, produces only by means of the portion of truth which it contains.
author: Mme. Swetchine

text: The secret of success is constancy to purpose.
author: Disraeli

text: The wealth of both Indies seems in great part but an accessory to the command of the seas.
author: Bacon

text: Transitory is all human work, small in itself, contemptible; only the worker thereof and the spirit that dwelt in him is significant.
author: Carlyle

text: Each man sees over his own experience a certain stain of error, whilst that of other men looks fair and ideal.
author: Emerson

text: Nobody should be rich but those who understand it.
author: Goethe

text: Our grand business is not to see what lies dimly at a distance, but to do what lies clearly at hand.
author: Carlyle

text: Many men attain a knowledge of what is perfect, and of their own insufficiency, and go on doing things by halves to the end of their days.
author: Goethe

text: Root away / The noisome weeds, which without profit suck / The soil's fertility from wholesome flowers.
author: Rich. II

text: Sundays observe; think when the bells do chime, / 'Tis angels' music, therefore come not late.
author: George Herbert

text: A last judgment is necessary, because fools flourish.
author: Wm. Blake

text: Life is a rich strain of music suggesting a realm too fair to be.
author: G. W. Curtis

text: Youth is full of sport, age's breath is short; / Youth is nimble, age is lame: / Youth is hot and bold, age is weak and cold; / Youth is wild, and age is tame.
author: Shakespeare

text: The young mind is naturally pliable and imitative, but in a more advanced state it grows rigid, and must be warmed and softened before it will receive a deep impression.
author: Joshua Reynolds

text: Passions may not unfitly be termed the mob of the man, that commits a riot upon his reason.
author: Wm. Penn

text: The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the well-spring of wisdom as a flowing brook.
author: Bible

text: The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason.
author: Bible

text: It is a strange habit of wise humanity to speak in enigmas only.
author: Ruskin

text: Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice.
author: Jesus

text: We love to see wisdom in unpretending forms, to recognise her royal features under a week-day vesture.
author: Carlyle

text: Private judgment with the accent on "private" is self-will; but with the accent on "judgment," it is freedom, free-will.
author: J. Hutchison Stirling

text: Yours is a pauper's soul, a rich man's pelf: / Rich to your heirs, a pauper to yourself.
author: Lucillius

text: Beautiful it is to understand and know that a thought did never yet die; that as thou, the originator thereof, hast gathered it and created it from the whole past, so thou wilt transmit to the whole future.
author: Carlyle

text: For just experience tells, in every soil, / That those that think must govern those that toil.
author: Goldsmith

text: I want that glib and oily art, / To speak and purpose not; since what I well intend, / I'll do't before I speak.
author: King Lear

text: Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.
author: Bible

text: Suffering which falls to our lot in the course of nature, or by chance or fate, does not, "ceteris paribus," seem so painful as suffering which is inflicted on us by the arbitrary will of another.
author: Schopenhauer

text: That learning which thou gettest by thy own observation and experience is far beyond that which thou gettest by precept; as the knowledge of a traveller exceeds that which is got by reading.
author: Thomas à Kempis

text: The gain of lying is nothing else but not to be trusted of any, nor to be believed when we say the truth.
author: Sir Walter Raleigh

text: Great men are not always wise.
author: Bible

text: Stronger than steel / Is the sword of the spirit; / Swifter than arrows / The life of the truth is; / Greater than anger / Is love, and subdueth.
author: Longfellow

text: If fun is good, truth is still better, and love most of all.
author: Thackeray

text: Power, like a desolating pestilence, / Pollutes whate'er it touches; and obedience, / Bane of all genius, virtue, freedom, truth, / Makes slaves of men, and of the human frame a mechanized automaton.
author: Shelley

text: Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
author: Bible

text: Truth, like the juice of a poppy, in small quantities, calms men; in larger, heats and irritates them, and is attended by fatal consequences in its excess.
author: Landor

text: Every man without passions has within him no principle of action nor motive to act.
author: Helvetius

text: Search not to find what lies too deeply hid; / Nor to know things whose knowledge is forbid.
author: Denham

text: Generosity, wrong placed, becomes a vice. A princely mind will undo a private family.
author: Fuller

text: Two misfortunes are twice as many at least as are needful to be talked over at one time.
author: Sterne

text: Practice aims at what is immediate; speculation at what is remote. author: Buckle

text: The secret of success in society is a certain heartiness and sympathy.
author: Emerson

text: The meteor flag of England, / Shall yet terrific burn, / Till danger's troubled night depart, / And the star of peace return.
author: Campbell

text: The wise man must go to the foolish, else would his wisdom go for nought, since the foolish never come to the wise.
author: Bodenstedt

text: Speak not at all till you have somewhat to speak; and care simply and with undivided mind for the truth of your speaking.
author: Carlyle

text: To the wisest man, wide as is his vision, Nature remains of quite infinite depth, of quite infinite expansion; and all experience thereof limits itself to some few computed centuries and measured square miles.
author: Carlyle

text: In the works of many celebrated authors men are mere personifications. We have not a jealous man, but jealousy; not a traitor, but perfidy; not a patriot, but patriotism. The mind of Bunyan, on the contrary, was so imaginative that personifications, when he dealt with them, became men.
author: Macaulay

text: Time is eternity, / Pregnant with all eternity can give.
author: Young

text: It is a maxim of those who are esteemed perfect, that abundance is the perverter of reason.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Romance is the truth of imagination and boyhood. Homer's horses clear the world at a bound. The child's eye needs no horizon to its prospect.... The palace that grew up in a night merely awakens a wish to live in it. The impossibilities of fifty years are the common-places of five.
author: Willmott

text: To improve the golden moment of opportunity, and catch the good that is within our reach, is the great art of life.
author: Johnson

text: When Nature fills the sails, the vessel goes smoothly on; and when judgment is the pilot, the insurance need not be high.
author: Sir T. Browne

text: A fool resents good counsel, but a wise man lays it to heart.
author: Confucius

text: The seat of knowledge is in the head; of wisdom, in the heart. We are sure to judge wrong if we do not feel aright.
author: Hazlitt

text: The rich man is seldom in his own halls, because it bores him to be there, and still he returns thither, because he is no better off outside.
author: Schopenhauer

text: For gold the merchant ploughs the main, / The farmer ploughs the manor; / But glory is the soldier's prize, / The soldier's wealth is honour.
author: Burns

text: War suspends the rules of moral obligation, and what is long suspended is in danger of being totally abrogated.
author: Burke

text: Good luck is the willing handmaid of upright, energetic character, and conscientious observance of duty.
author: Lowell

text: They asked Lucman the fabulist, "From whom did you learn manners?" He answered, "From the unmannerly."
author: Saadi

text: He who will work aright must not trouble himself about what is ill done, but only do well himself.
author: Goethe

text: Theirs not to make reply, / Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do or die.
author: Tennyson

text: Fortitude is to be seen in toils and dangers; temperance in the denial of sensual pleasures; prudence in the choice between good and evil; justice in awarding to every one his due.
author: Cic

text: Patience is a remedy for every sorrow.
author: Pub. Syr

text: Every healthy effort is directed from the inward to the outward world.
author: Goethe

text: Chance is the providence of adventurers.
author: Napoleon

text: Solitude can be well applied and sit right upon but very few persons. They must have knowledge of the world to see the follies of it, and virtue enough to despise all the vanity.
author: Cowley

text: Old men lose one of the most precious rights of man, that of being judged by their peers.
author: Goethe

text: The schoolboy counts the time till the return of the holidays; the minor longs to be of age; the lover is impatient till he is married.
author: Addison

text: The fatal man, is he not always the unthinking, the man who cannot think and see?
author: Carlyle

text: In all provinces there are artists and artisans; men who labour mechanically in a department, without eye for the whole, not feeling that there is a whole; and men who inform and ennoble the humblest department with an idea of the whole, and habitually know that only in the whole is the partial to be truly discerned.
author: Carlyle

text: When all is done, the help of good counsel is that which setteth business straight.
author: Bacon

text: That which, intellectually considered, we call Reason, considered in relation to nature we call Spirit.
author: Emerson

text: Wealth is the possession of useful articles which we can use, (so that) instead of depending merely on a "have," it is thus seen to depend on a "can."
author: Ruskin

text: So thou be above it, make the world serve thy purpose, but do not thou serve it.
author: Goethe

text: We are not to be astonished that the wise walk more slowly in their road to virtue than fools in their passage to vice; since passion drags us along, while wisdom only points out the way.
author: Confucius

text: A courage to endure and to obey.
author: Tennyson

text: Justice of thought and style, refinement in manners, good breeding, and politeness of every kind, can come only from the trial and experience of what is best.
author: Duncan

text: Think you, 'mid all this mighty sum / Of things for ever speaking, / That nothing of itself will come, / But we must still be seeking.
author: Wordsworth

text: Nothing is superficial to a deep observer. It is in trifles that the mind betrays itself.
author: Bulwer Lytton

text: Light is the symbol of truth.
author: Lowell

text: Things fasten upon thee only according as the degree of thy own love and inclination for them gives opportunity and advantage.
author: Thomas à Kempis

text: They who resign life rather than part with liberty do only a prudent action; but those who lay it down for friends and country do a heroic one.
author: Steele

text: To be disobedient through temptation is human sin; but to be disobedient for the sake of disobedience, fiendish sin. To be obedient for the sake of success in conduct is human virtue; to be obedient for the sake of obedience, angelic virtue.

text: Silence is the sleep that nourishes wisdom.
author: Bacon

text: The dictum that truth always triumphs over persecution is one of those pleasant falsehoods ... which all experience refutes. History teems with instances of truth put down by persecution. If not suppressed for ever, it may be thrown back for centuries.

text: Who, in the midst of just provocation to anger, instantly finds the fit word which settles all around him in silence, is more than wise or just; he is, were he a beggar, of more than royal blood—he is of celestial descent.

text: When a man gives himself up to the government of a ruling passion—or, in other words, when his hobby-horse grows headstrong—farewell cool reason and fair discretion!
