text: Grief should be the instructor of the wise; / Sorrow is knowledge: they who know the most / Must mourn the deepest o'er the fatal truth, / The Tree of Knowledge is not that of Life.

text: Every heroic act measures itself by its contempt of some external good; but it finds its own success at last, and then the prudent also extol.
author: Emerson

text: The errors of a wise man make your rule / Rather than the perfections of a fool.
author: Wm. Blake

text: To fight with its neighbours never was, and is now less than ever, the real trade of England.
author: Carlyle

text: Evil men understand not judgment, but they that seek the Lord understand all things.
author: Bible

text: The history of a soldier's wound beguiles the pain of it. We lose the right of complaining sometimes by forbearing it, but we often treble the force.
author: Sterne

text: There is no other revelation than the thoughts of the wise.
author: Schopenhauer

text: Science does not know its debt to imagination.
author: Emerson

text: The one enemy we have in this universe is stupidity, darkness of mind; of which darkness there are many sources, every sin a source, and probably self-conceit the chief source.

text: The new man is always in a new time, under new conditions; his course is the fac-simile of no prior one, but is by its nature original.
author: Carlyle

text: Craftiness is a quality in the mind and a vice in the character.
author: Sanial Dubay

text: Talk that does not end in action is better suppressed altogether.
author: Carlyle

text: Humour is properly the exponent of low things; that which first renders them poetical to the mind.
author: Carlyle

text: Truth, like the Venus de Medici, will pass down in thirty fragments to posterity; but posterity will collect and recompose them into a goddess.
author: Richter

text: What signifies the loss of a Hercules even to the loss of an idea?
author: Ed

text: The soul, / Though made in time, survives for aye; / And, though it hath beginning, sees no end.
author: Sir J. Davies

text: Though the heavens fall, the orbs of truth and justice fall not.
author: J. Burroughs

text: Physical courage, which despises all danger, will make a man brave in one way; and moral courage, which defies all opinion, will make a man brave in another.
author: Colton

text: What you do not risk all to part with thou hast not loved and possessed entirely.
author: J. G. Fisher

text: Never by reflection, only by doing what it lies on him to do, is self-knowledge possible to any man.
author: Goethe

text: Wanton jests make fools laugh and wise men frown.
author: Fuller

text: Learning passes for wisdom among them who want both.
author: Sir W. Temple

text: Time is but a stream I go a-fishing in. I drink at it; but while I drink I see the sandy bottom, and detect how shallow it is. Its thin current slides away, but eternity remains. I would drink deeper, fish in the sky, whose bottom is pebbly with stars.
author: Thoreau

text: Find fault, when you must find fault, in private, if possible, and some time after the offence, rather than at the time.
author: Sydney Smith

text: It is wisdom alone that can recognise wisdom.
author: Carlyle

text: Positiveness is a good quality for preachers and orators, because whoever would obtrude his thoughts and reasons upon a multitude, win convince others the more as he appears convinced himself.
author: Swift

text: The spiritual is ever the inner in a man becoming outer, the invisible becoming visible, the supernatural becoming natural, the infinite becoming finite, and the eternal veiling itself in the guise of time; never an emancipation from the flesh, but ever an incarnation in flesh.

text: The feast of reason and the flow of soul.
author: Pope

text: Men commonly think according to their inclinations, speak according to their learning and imbibed opinions, but generally act according to custom.
author: Bacon

text: Lips never err when wisdom keeps the door.
author: Delaune

text: Vain man would be wise, though man be born like a wild ass's colt.
author: Bible

text: Dost thou love life? Then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of.
author: B. Franklin

text: Our delight in reason degenerates into idolatry of the herald.
author: Emerson

text: The first business of the philosopher is to part with self-conceit.
author: Epictetus

text: If speculation tends to a terrific unity, in which all things are absorbed, action tends directly backwards to diversity.
author: Emerson

text: Temperance is a bridle of gold.
author: Burton

text: Man's body and his mind are exactly like a jerkin and a jerkin's lining—rumple the one, you rumple the other.
author: Sterne

text: The disease with which the human mind now labours is want of faith.
author: Emerson

text: Politicians think that by stopping up the chimney they can stop its smoking. They try the experiment; they drive the smoke back, and there is more smoke than ever.
author: Borne

text: There are certain times in our life when we find ourselves in circumstances, that not only press upon us, but seem to weigh us down altogether. author: Goethe

text: If aged and life-weary men have called to their neighbours: "Think of dying!" we younger and life-loving men may well keep encouraging and reminding one another with the cheerful words: "Think of wandering!"
author: Goethe

text: Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
author: Jesus

text: Work is the cure for all the maladies and miseries of man—honest work, which you intend getting done.
author: Carlyle

text: Genius is not a single power, but a combination of great powers. It reasons, but it is not reasoning; it judges, but it is not judgment; imagines, but it is not imagination; it feels deeply and fiercely, but it is not passion. It is neither, because it is all.
author: Whipple

text: Time dissipates to shining ether the solid angularity of facts.
author: Emerson

text: It is with diseases of the mind as with those of the body; we are half dead before we understand our disorders, and half cured when we do.
author: Colton

text: Everything runs to excess; every good quality is noxious if unmixed; and to carry the danger to the edge of ruin, Nature causes each man's peculiarity to superabound.
author: Emerson

text: Natural abilities are like natural plants, that need pruning by study; and studies themselves do give forth directions too much at large, except they be bounded in by experience.
author: Bacon

text: Knowledge is the treasure of the mind, but discretion is the key to it, without which it is useless. The practical part of wisdom is the best.
author: Feltham

text: If you wish to astonish the whole world, tell the simple truth.
author: Rahel

text: Since time is not a person we can overtake when he is past, let us honour him with mirth and cheerfulness of heart while he is passing.
author: Goethe

text: He is a hard man who is only just, and he a sad man who is only wise.
author: Voltaire

text: Human action is a seed of circumstances scattered in the dark land of the future and hopefully left to the powers that rule human destiny.
author: Schiller

text: What we hope ever to do with ease we may learn first to do with diligence.
author: Johnson

text: Poets lose half the praise they should have got, / Could it be known what they discreetly blot.
author: Waller

text: Subdue fate, and exert human strength to the utmost of your power; and if, when pains have been taken, success attend not, in whom is the blame?
author: Hitopadesa

text: Only learn to catch happiness, for happiness is ever by you.
author: Goethe

text: Falsehood is so much the more commendable, by how much more it resembles truth, and is the more pleasing the more it is doubtful and possible.
author: Cervantes

text: They that will crowd about bonfires may, sometimes very fairly, get their beards singed; it is the price they pay for such illumination; natural twilight is safe and free to all.
author: Carlyle

text: It is the greatest invention man has ever made, this of marking down the unseen thought that is in him by written characters.
author: Carlyle

text: What love hides is raised as from the dead / Some day, and kills the love which covered it, / And frankest truth is more than subtle wit.
author: Dr. Walter Smith

text: Soldiers! what I have to offer you is fatigue, danger, struggle, and death; the chill of the cold night in the free air, and heat under the burning sun; no lodgings, no munitions, no provisions, but forced marches, dangerous watchposts, and the continual struggle with the bayonet against batteries. Those who love freedom and their country may follow me!
author: Kossuth

text: Let us make haste to live, since every day to a wise man is a new life.
author: Sen

text: Stillness of person and steadiness of features are signal marks of good breeding. Vulgar persons can't sit still, or at least they must work their limbs or features.
author: Holmes

text: Nearly all our powerful men in this age of the world are unbelievers; the best of them in doubt and misery; the plurality in plodding hesitation, doing, as well as they can, what practical work lies ready to their hands.
author: Ruskin

text: Riches do not consist in having more gold and silver, but in having more in proportion than our neighbours.
author: Locke

text: One man that has a higher wisdom in him is not stronger than ten men, or than ten thousand, but than all men that have it not.
author: Carlyle

text: Reason's glimmering ray / Was lent, not to assure our doubtful way, / But guide us upward to a better day.
author: Dryden

text: When clouds appear, wise men put on their cloaks; / When great leaves fall, the winter is at hand.
author: Rich. III

text: Wisdom sits with children round her knees.
author: Wordsworth

text: Uttered out of time, or concealed in its season, good savoureth of evil.
author: Tupper

text: Never a tear bedims the eye / That time and patience will not dry; / Never a lip is curved in pain / That can't be kissed into smiles again.
author: Bret Harte

text: Vain, very vain, my weary search to find / That bliss which only centres in the mind.
author: Goldsmith

text: What is a man profited if he shall gain the whole world and lose his own soul?
author: Jesus

text: No art can be noble which is incapable of expressing thought, and no art is capable of expressing thought which does not change.
author: Ruskin

text: The king's favour is toward a wise servant.
author: Bible

text: Rather to do nothing than to do good is the lowest state of a degraded mind.
author: Johnson

text: Judicious persons will think all the less of us because of the ill-judged praises of our silly friends.
author: Spurgeon

text: Private affection bereaves us easily of a right judgment.
author: Thomas à Kempis

text: All public disorder proceeds from want of work.
author: Courier

text: We should never risk pleasantry except with well-bred people, and people with brains.
author: La Bruyère

text: Poetry is the offspring of the rarest beauty, begot by imagination upon thought, and clad by taste and fancy in habiliments of grace.
author: Simms

text: There are two ways of attaining an important end—force and perseverance; the silent power of the latter grows irresistible with time.
author: Mme. Swetchine

text: When speech is given to a soul holy and true, time and its dome of ages becomes as a mighty whispering-gallery, round which the imprisoned utterance runs, and reverberates forever.
author: James Martineau

text: Cautious age suspects the flattering form, and only credits what experience tells.
author: Johnson

text: The strong man is the wise man; the man with the gift of method, of faithfulness, of valour; who has insight into what is what, into what will follow out of what, the eye to see and the hand to do.
author: Carlyle

text: Falsehood is never so successful as when she baits her hook with truth.
author: Colton

text: Poetry is inspiration; has in it a certain spirituality and divinity which no dissecting knife will discover; arises in the most secret and most sacred region of man's soul, as it were in our Holy of Holies; and as for external things, depends only on such as can operate in that region; among which it will be found that Acts of Parliament and the state of Smithfield Markets nowise play the chief parts.
author: Carlyle

text: Where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
author: St. James

text: No doubt every person is entitled to make and to think as much of himself as possible, only he ought not to worry others about this, for they have enough to do with and in themselves, if they too are to be of some account, both now and hereafter.
author: Goethe

text: Reason cannot show itself more reasonable than to cease reasoning on things above reason.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: The man of wisdom is the man of years.
author: Young

text: The rich becoming richer and the poor poorer, is the cry throughout the whole civilised world.
author: Sillar

text: From the beginning and to the end of time, Love reads without letters and counts without arithmetic.
author: Ruskin

text: "Win hearts," said Burleigh to Queen Elizabeth, "and you have all men's hearts and purses."
author: Smiles

text: Ever must pain urge us to labour, and only in free effort can any blessedness be imagined for us.
author: Carlyle

text: Truth has no gradations; nothing which admits of increase can be so much what it is as truth is truth. There may be a strange thing, and a thing more strange; but if a proposition be true, there can be none more true.
author: Johnson

text: Who questioneth much, shall learn much, and content much.
author: Bacon

text: Men of true wisdom and goodness are contented to take persons and things as they are, without complaining of their imperfections or attempting to amend them.
author: Fielding

text: I think a lock and key a security at least equal to the bosom of any friend whatever.
author: Burns

text: Only great men have any business with great defects.
author: La Roche

text: If we are told a man is religious, we still ask what are his morals; but if we hear he has honest morals, we seldom think of the other question, whether he be religious.

text: Trust instinct to the end, though you can render no reason.

text: The great man goes ahead of his time, the prudent man goes with it, the crafty man makes his own out of it, and the blockhead sets himself against it.

text: Labour is the instituted means for the methodical development of all our powers under the direction and control of the will.
author: J. G. Holland

text: If we love those we lose, can we altogether lose those we love?

text: Things will always right themselves in time, if only those who know what they want to do, and can do, persevere unremittingly in work and action.

text: A good thought is a great boon.
author: Bovee

text: Say not, I will do so to him as he hath done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.

text: What is everybody's business is nobody's business.
author: Izaak Walton

author: Bible

text: The aim of life is work, or there is no aim at all.

author: Ruskin

text: There is no work of genius which has not been the delight of mankind, no word of genius to which the human heart and soul have not, sooner or later, responded.

author: Thoreau

author: Dryden

text: Those who make the worst use of their time most complain of its shortness.

text: Pride, ill-nature, and want of sense are the three great sources of ill-manners; without some one of these defects no man will behave himself ill for want of experience, or what, in the language of fools, is called knowing the world.

author: Goethe

author: Froude

text: Silence is the mother of truth.
author: Disraeli

text: Buy the truth, and sell it not.
author: Bible

author: Jean Paul

text: In peace, who is not wise?

author: Burns

author: Sen

text: I must work the work of Him that sent me while it is day; the night cometh when no man can work.

author: Dickens

text: Real action is in silent moments.

text: Poverty consists in feeling poor.

text: Nought treads so silent as the foot of time.

text: A beast that wants discourse of reason.

text: Hope not wholly to reason away your troubles; but do not feed them with attention, and they will die imperceptibly away.

text: Constant thought will overflow in words unconsciously.

text: Work was made for man, and not man for work.

text: Singularity shows something wrong in the mind.

text: Grace is to the body what good sense is to the mind.

text: Truth is the highest thing that man may keep.

text: That which can be done with perfect convenience and without loss, is not always the thing that most needs to be done, or which we are most imperatively required to do.
author: Ruskin

text: Though ambition in itself is a vice, yet it is often the parent of virtues.
author: Quinct

text: Waft yourselves, yearning souls, upon the stars; / Sow yourselves on the wandering winds of space; / Watch patient all your days, if your eyes take / Some dim, cold ray of knowledge. The dull world / Hath need of you—the purblind, slothful world!
author: Lewis Morris

text: Let not mercy and truth forsake thee.
author: Bible

text: Leisure is time for doing something useful; this leisure the diligent man will obtain; the lazy man never.
author: Ben. Franklin

text: Authors may be divided into falling stars, planets, and fixed stars: the first have a momentary effect; the second, a much longer duration; and the third are unchangeable, possess their own light, and shine for all time.
author: Schopenhauer

text: We can take up no scheme, however wild and impracticable, but it will strike off some flower or fruit from the tree of knowledge.
author: Ward Beecher

text: He is oft the wisest man / Who is not wise at all.
author: Wordsworth

text: History, as it lies at the root of all science, is also the first distinct product of man's spiritual nature, his earliest expression of what may be called thought.
author: Carlyle

text: Wonder is from surprise, and surprise ceases upon experience.
author: South

text: Whatever befalls us, though it is wise to be serious, it is useless and foolish, and perhaps sinful, to be gloomy.
author: Johnson

text: We never can know the truth of sin; for its nature is to deceive alike on the one side the sinner and on the other the judge.
author: Ruskin

text: The mind's the standard of the man.
author: Watts

text: Order is truth, each thing standing on the basis that belongs to it.
author: Carlyle

text: It is certain my belief gains quite infinitely the moment I can convince another mind thereof.
author: Novalis

text: Success in war, like charity in religion, covers a multitude of sins.
author: Sir C. Napier

text: My soul, what's lighter than a feather? Wind. / Than wind? The fire. And what than fire? The mind. / What's lighter than the mind? A thought. Than thought? / This bubble world. What than this bubble? Nought.
author: Quarles

text: Youth is not the age of pleasure; we then expect too much, and we are therefore exposed to daily disappointments and mortifications. When we are a little older, and have brought down our wishes to our experience, then we become calm and begin to enjoy ourselves.
author: Lord Liverpool

text: Man was created to work—not to speculate, or feel, or dream.
author: Carlyle

text: A strong memory is generally joined to a weak judgment.
author: Montaigne

text: When pride cometh, then cometh shame; but with the lowly is wisdom.
author: Bible

text: Be wise with speed; / A fool at forty is a fool indeed.
author: Young

text: We estimate great men by their virtue, not by their success.
author: Corn. Nep

text: The invariable mark of wisdom is to see the miraculous in the common.
author: Emerson

text: He who has no vision of Eternity will never get a true hold of Time.
author: Carlyle

text: Learning itself, received into a mind / By nature weak or viciously inclined, / Serves but to lead philosophers astray, / Where children would with ease discern the way.
author: Cowper

text: There are single thoughts that contain the essence of a whole volume, single sentences that have the beauties of a large work.
author: Joubert

text: Every thought was once a poem.
author: Emerson

text: Experience teaches us again and again that there is nothing men have less command over than their tongues.
author: Spinoza

text: Mentally and bodily endowed men are the most modest, while, on the other hand, all who have some peculiar mental defect think a great deal more of themselves.
author: Goethe

text: Penetration has an air of divination; it pleases our vanity more than any other quality of the mind.
author: La Roche

text: Knowledge is to one a goddess, to another only an excellent cow.
author: Schiller

text: Morals are generated as the atmosphere is. 'Tis a secret the genesis of either; but the springs of justice and courage do not fail any more than salt or sulphur springs.
author: Emerson

text: If in the course of our life we see that done by others for which we ourselves at one time felt a vocation, and which we were, with much else, compelled to relinquish, then the noble feeling comes in, that only humanity altogether is the true man, and that the individual can only rejoice and be happy when he has the heart to feel himself in the whole.
author: Goethe

text: The human mind, in proportion as it is deprived of external resources, sedulously labours to find within itself the means of happiness, learns to rely with confidence on its own exertions, and gains with greater certainty the power of being happy.
author: Zimmermann

text: Make thick my blood, / Stop up the access and passage to remorse, / That no compunctious visitings of Nature / Shake my fell purpose.
author: Macb

text: Poetry is the art of uniting pleasure with truth by calling imagination to the help of reason.
author: Johnson

text: Architecture is the work of nations.
author: Ruskin

text: Custom does often reason overrule, / And only serves for reason to the fool.
author: Rochester

text: Economy does not consist in the reckless reduction of estimates; on the contrary, such a course almost necessarily tends to increased expenditure. There can be no economy where there is no efficiency.
author: Disraeli

text: There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face.
author: Macb

text: As reason is a rebel unto faith, so is passion unto reason.
author: Sir T. Browne

text: Health is the condition of wisdom, and the sign is cheerfulness—an open and noble temper.
author: Emerson

text: To threats the stubborn sinner oft is hard, / Wrapp'd in his crimes, against the storm prepared; / But, when the milder beams of mercy play, / He melts, and throws his cumbrous cloak away.
author: Dryden

text: Truth does not consist in minute accuracy of detail, but in conveying a right impression; and there are vague ways of speaking that are truer than strict facts would be. When the Psalmist said, "Rivers of water run down mine eyes, because men keep not thy law," he did not state the fact but he stated a truth deeper than fact and truer.
author: Dean Alford

text: Pedantry is properly overrating any kind of knowledge we pretend to.
author: Swift

text: The prudence of the best of hearts is often defeated by the tenderness of the best of hearts.
author: Fielding

text: Truth may lie in laughter, and wisdom in a jest.
author: Dr. W. Smith

text: We look before and after, / And pine for what is not; / E'en our sincerest laughter / With some pain is fraught; / Our sweetest songs are those which tell of saddest thought.
author: Shelley

text: Shall we repine at a little misplaced charity, when an all-knowing, all-wise Being showers down every day his benefits on the unthankful and undeserving?
author: Atterbury

text: Some folk's tongues are like the clocks as run on strikin', not to tell you the time o' the day, but because there's summat wrong i' their inside.
author: George Eliot

text: A single word is often a concentrated poem, a little grain of pure gold, capable of being beaten out into a broad extent of gold-leaf.
author: Trench

text: To be happy is not the purpose of our being, but to deserve happiness.
author: Fichte

text: And he is oft the wisest man / Who is not wise at all.
author: Wordsworth

text: That elevation of mind which we see in moments of peril, if it is uncontrolled by justice, and strives only for its own advantage, becomes a crime.
author: Cic

text: Modest doubt is called / The beacon of the wise, the tent that searches / To the bottom of the worst.
author: Troil. and Cres

text: A man with knowledge but without energy, is a house furnished but not inhabited; a man with energy but no knowledge, a house dwelt in but unfurnished.
author: John Sterling

text: Enjoy what thou hast inherited from thy sires if thou wouldst possess it; what we employ not is an oppressive burden; what the moment brings forth, that only can it profit by.
author: Goethe

text: Knowledge is not happiness, and science but an exchange of ignorance for that which is another kind of ignorance.
author: Byron

text: The manifestation of one's own superiority may render the purchase too dear, by being bought at the terrible price of our neighbour's dislike.
author: Lover

text: There is a time in every man's education when he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance.
author: Emerson

text: Fare you weel, auld Nickie-ben! / O wad ye tak' a thocht and men'! / Ye aiblins micht—I dinna ken—/ Still hae a stake: / I'm wae to think upo' yon den, / E'en for your sake.
author: Burns

text: Let every thought too, soldier-like, be stripped, / And roughly looked over.
author: P. J. Bailey

text: Worldly riches are like nuts; many clothes are torn in getting them, many a tooth broke in cracking them, but never a belly filled with eating them.
author: R. Venning

text: He was not of an age, but for all Time, / Sweet Swan of Avon.
author: Ben Jonson

text: Fine feelings, without vigour of reason, are in the situation of the extreme feathers of a peacock's tail—dragging in the mud.
author: John Foster

text: The seed of knowledge ripens but slowly in the mind, but the flowers grow quickly.
author: Bodenstedt

text: A last judgment is not for making bad men better, but for hindering them from oppressing the good.
author: Wm. Blake

text: Whoso lives for humanity must be content to lose himself.
author: O. B. Frothingham

text: Take from the philosopher the pleasure of being heard, and his desire for knowledge ceases.
author: Rousseau

text: Nothing deepens and intensifies family traits like poverty and toil and suffering. It is the furnace heat that brings out the characters, the pressure that makes the strata perfect.
author: John Burroughs

text: Though thousands hate physic, because of the cost, / Yet thousands it helpeth, that else should be lost.
author: Thomas Tusser

text: There is a certain artificial polish, a commonplace vivacity, acquired by perpetually mingling in the beau monde, which, in the commerce of the world, supplies the place of natural suavity and good-humour; but it is purchased at the expense of all original and sterling traits of character.
author: Washington Irving

text: I am amazed, methinks, and lose my way / Among the thorns and dangers of the world.
author: King John

text: Men are often capable of greater things than they perform. They are sent into the world with bills of credit, and seldom draw to their full extent.
author: Walpole

text: You traverse the world in search of happiness, which is within the reach of every man; a contented mind confers it on all.
author: Hor

text: The superstition in which we have grown up does not lose its hold over us even when we recognise it for such. Those who scoff at their fetters are not all free men.
author: Lessing

text: Humility is the only true wisdom by which we prepare our minds for all the possible vicissitudes of life.
author: Arliss' Lit. Col

text: Small curses upon great occasions are but so much waste of our strength and soul's health to no manner of purpose; they are like sparrow-shot fired against a bastion.
author: Sterne

text: Cruelty in war buyeth conquest at the dearest price.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: Riches amassed in haste will diminish; but those collected by hand and little by little will multiply.
author: Goethe

text: A man protesting against error is on the way towards uniting himself with all men that believe in truth.
author: Carlyle

text: Think not thy fame at every twitch will break; / By great deeds show that thou canst little do; / And do them not; that shall thy wisdom be; / And change thy temperance into bravery.
author: George Herbert

text: In the fact that hero-worship exists, has existed, and will for ever exist universally among mankind, mayest thou discern the cornerstone of living rock, whereon all politics for the remotest time may stand secure.
author: Carlyle

text: The beginning of all good law, and nearly the end of it, is that every man shall do good work for his bread, and that every man shall have good bread for his work.
author: Ruskin

text: Wealth without contentment climbs a hill, / To feel those tempests which fly over ditches.
author: George Herbert

text: From ignorance our comfort flows; / The only wretched are the wise.
author: Prior

text: Come what come may, / Time and the hour runs through the roughest day.
author: Macb

text: Earnestness is enthusiasm tempered by reason.
author: Pascal

text: For one person who can think, there are at least a hundred who can observe. An accurate observer is, no doubt, rare; but an accurate thinker is far rarer.
author: Buckle

text: Ridicule intrinsically is a small faculty; we may say, the smallest of all faculties that other men are at the pains to repay with any esteem. author: Carlyle

text: Society has always a destructive influence upon an artist:—by its sympathy with his meanest powers; secondly, by its chilling want of understanding of his greatest; and, thirdly, by its vain occupation of his time and thoughts.
author: Ruskin

text: Courage and modesty are the most unequivocal of virtues, for they are of a kind that hypocrisy cannot imitate.
author: Goethe

text: Gifts from the hand are silver and gold, but the heart gives that which neither silver nor gold can buy.
author: Ward Beecher

text: It is not because of his toils that I lament for the poor; we must all toil, or steal, which is worse; no faithful workman finds his task a pastime.... author: Carlyle

text: But truths on which depend our main concern, / That 'tis our shame and misery not to learn, / Shine by the side of every path we tread, / With such a lustre, he that runs may read.
author: Cowper

text: Why tell me that a man is a fine speaker if it is not the truth that he is speaking? If an eloquent speaker is not speaking the truth, is there a more horrid kind of object in creation?
author: Carlyle

text: Have more than thou showest; / Speak less than thou knowest; / Lend less than thou owest; / Learn more than thou trowest; / Set less than thou throwest.
author: King Lear

text: Praise, like gold and diamonds, owes its value only to its scarcity.
author: Johnson

text: Let us be poised, and wise, and our own to-day.
author: Emerson

text: Flowers of rhetoric in sermons and serious discourses are like the blue and red flowers in corn, pleasing to those who come only for amusement, but prejudicial to him who would reap profit from it.
author: Pope

text: Be wisely worldly; be not worldly wise.
author: Quarles

text: What is noble?—That which places / Truth in its enfranchised will, / Leaving steps, like angel-traces, / That mankind may follow still!
author: C. Swain

text: What is strength without a double share / Of wisdom? vast, unwieldy, burdensome, / Proudly secure, yet liable to fall / By weakest subtleties; not made to rule, / But to subserve where wisdom bears command.
author: Milton

text: Few have wealth, but all must have a home.
author: Emerson

text: To conquer without danger would be to conquer without glory.
author: Corneille

text: Law that shocks equity is reason's murderer.
author: A, Hill

text: Whosoever will save his life shall lose it; and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.
author: Jesus

text: We have nothing to do with what is happening in space (or possibly may happen in time); we have only to attend to what is happening here—and now.
author: Ruskin

text: What governs men is the fear of truth, except such as is useful to them.
author: Amiel

text: Work is only done well when it is done with a will.
author: Ruskin

text: Thinking is but an idle waste of thought; / For nought is everything, and everything is nought.
author: Smith, "Rejected Addresses."

text: Screw your courage to the sticking-place, / And we'll not fail.
author: Macb

text: Time is trouble and the author of destruction; he seizeth even from afar.
author: Hitopadesa

text: The faith in an Invisible, Unnameable, Godlike, present everywhere in all we see and work and suffer, is the essence of all faith whatsoever; and that once denied, or, still worse, asserted with lips only, and out of bound prayer-books only, what other thing remains credible?
author: Carlyle

text: Wisdom's path is steep; but, gained the height, / The Muse's gifts will fill you with delight.
author: Onestes

text: It is the curse of talent, that, though it works more surely and persistently than genius, it reaches no goal; while genius, hovering for long on the summit of the ideal, looks round, smiling, far above.

text: Virtue which is according to the precepts of reason, appears equally great in avoiding as in overcoming dangers.

text: What glitters is for the moment; the genuine is for all time.

text: Truth being weighed against a thousand Aswamedha sacrifices, was found to be of more consequence than the whole thousand offerings.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Never talk half a minute without pausing and giving others an opportunity to strike in.
author: Sydney Smith

text: If we are rich with the riches which we neither give nor enjoy, we are rich with the riches which are buried in the caverns of the earth.
author: Hitopadesa

text: It is generally a sign of a small mind to think differently from great minds.
author: Goethe

text: Whoever would persuade men to religion both with art and efficacy, must found the persuasion of it upon this, that it interferes not with any rational pleasure, that it bids nobody quit the enjoyment of any one thing that his reason can prove to him ought to be enjoyed.

text: Knowledge is boundless; human capacity limited.
author: Chamfort

text: When rich villains have need of poor ones, poor ones may make what price they will.
author: Much Ado

text: What people call her history is not hers at all; but that of her kings (though the history of them is worth reading), or the tax-gatherers employed by them, which is as if people were to call Mr. Gladstone's history or Mr. Lowe's, yours or mine.

text: No knowledge is lost, but perfected, and changed for much nobler, sweeter, greater knowledge.
author: Baxter

text: The best preservative to keep the mind in health is the faithful admonition of a friend.
author: Bacon

text: Human courage should rise to the height of human calamity.
author: Gen. Lee

text: Within man is the soul of the whole; the wise silence, the universal beauty, to which every part and particle is equally related—the Eternal One.
author: Emerson

text: Glory relaxes often and debilitates the mind; censure stimulates and contracts—both to an extreme.
author: Shenstone

text: But far more numerous was the herd of such / Who think too little and who talk too much.
author: Dryden

author: J. C. Sharp

text: Let him who gropes painfully in darkness or uncertain light, and prays vehemently that the dawn may ripen into day, lay this precept well to heart: "Do the duty which lies nearest thee," which thou knowest to be a duty! Thy second duty will already have become clearer.
author: Carlyle

text: Virtue is an angel; but she is a blind one, and must ask of Knowledge to show her the pathway that leads to her goal. text: Sure as night follows day, / Death treads in pleasure's footsteps round the world, / When pleasure treads the path which reason shuns.
author: Young

text: Discontent is like ink poured into water, which fills the whole fountain full of blackness. It casts a cloud over the mind, and renders it more occupied about the evil which disquiets it than about the means of removing it.

text: There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth: and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
author: Bible

text: "Wouldst thou," so the helmsman answered, / "Learn the secret of the sea? / Only those who brave its dangers / Comprehend its mystery!"
author: Longfellow

text: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
author: Bible

text: Work till the last beam fadeth, / Fadeth to shine no more; / Work while the night is darkening, / When man's work is o'er.
author: Walker

text: Men of great parts are often unfortunate in the management of public business, because they are apt to go out of the common road by the quickness of their imagination.
author: Swift

text: Truth is the root, but human sympathy is the flower of practical life.
author: Chapin

text: It is not work that kills men, it is worry. It is not the revolution that destroys the machinery, but the friction.
author: Ward Beecher

text: Remember that you are an actor in a drama of such sort as the Author chooses. If short, then in a short one; if long, then in a long one. If it be His pleasure that you should act a poor man, see that you act it well; or a cripple, or a ruler, or a private citizen. For this is your business, to act well the given part; but to choose it, belongs to another.
author: Epictetus

text: If poverty is the mother of crimes, want of sense is the father of them.
author: La Bruyère

text: 'Tis my opinion 'tis necessary to be happy, that we think no place more agreeable than that where we are.
author: Lady Montagu

text: Truth provokes those whom it does not convert.
author: Bp. Wilson

text: The best way to come to truth is to examine things as they really are, and not to conclude they are, as we have been taught by others to imagine.
author: Locke

text: Was thy life given to thee / For making pretty sentences, and play / Of dainty humour for the mirthful heart / To be more merry, or to serve thy kind, / Redressing wrong?
author: Dr. W. Smith

text: I am afraid to think what I have done; / Look on't again I dare not.
author: Macb

text: Ideas often flash across our minds more complete than we could make them after much labour.
author: La Roche

text: One thought includes all thought, in the sense that a grain of sand includes the universe.
author: Coleridge

text: Mathematics can remove no prejudices and soften no obduracy. It has no influence in sweetening the bitter strife of parties, and in the moral world generally its action is perfectly null.
author: Goethe

text: Truth is to be loved purely and solely because it is true.
author: Carlyle

text: You often understand the true connection of important events in your life not while they are going on, nor soon after they are past, but only a considerable time afterwards.
author: Schopenhauer

text: The Highest not merely has, but is, reason and understanding.
author: Goethe

text: Wide our world displays its worth, man's strife and strife's success, / All the good and beauty, wonder crowning wonder, / Till my heart and soul applaud perfection, nothing less.
author: Browning

text: One is always making good use of one's time when engaged with a subject that daily forces one to make advances in self-culture.
author: Goethe

text: Labour is the Lethe of both past and present.
author: Jean Paul

text: Our / Virtues lie in the interpretation of the time.
author: Coriolanus

text: Dogmatic jargon, learn'd by heart, / Trite sentences, hard terms of art, / To vulgar ears seem so profound, / They fancy learning in the sound.
author: Gay

text: Nothing more readily pleases a vulgar mind than to find anomalies in conduct or character.
author: Alex. Whitelaw

text: It's no in titles nor in rank; / It's no in wealth like London bank, / To purchase peace and rest: / It's no in makin' muckle mair, / It's no in books, it's no in lear, / To mak' us truly blest.
author: Burns

text: In times of necessity the words of the wise are worthy to be observed.
author: Hitopadesa

text: Thou! why, thou wilt quarrel with a man that hath a hair more or a hair less in his beard than thou hast. Thou wilt quarrel with a man for cracking nuts, having no other reason but because thou hast hazel eyes.... Thy head is full of quarrels as an egg is full of meat.
author: Rom. and Jul

text: There's something good in all weathers. If it don't happen to be good for my work to-day, it's good for some other man's to-day, and will come round to me to-morrow.
author: Dickens

text: Happy contractedness of youth, nay, of mankind in general, that they think neither of the high nor the deep, of the true nor the false, but only of what is suited to their own conceptions.
author: Goethe

text: Full of wise saws and modern instances.
author: As You Like It

text: To act with a purpose is what raises man above the brutes; to invent with a purpose, to imitate with a purpose, is that which distinguishes genius from the petty artists who only invent to invent, and imitate to imitate.
author: Lessing

text: Life is made up, not of great sacrifices or duties, but of little things, in which smiles and kindness, and small obligations given habitually, are what win the heart and secure comfort.
author: Sir H. Davy

text: He that questioneth much will learn much.
author: Bacon

text: Most natures are insolvent; cannot satisfy their own wants, have an ambition out of all proportion to their practical force, and so do lean and beg day and night continually.
author: Emerson

text: Large fortunes cannot be made by the work of any one man's hands or head.
author: Ruskin

text: The popular man stands on our own level, or a hairsbreadth higher; and shows us a truth we can see without shifting our present intellectual position. The original man stands above us, and wishes to wrench us from our old fixtures, and elevate us to a higher and clearer level.
author: Carlyle

text: Keep me in patience; and, with ripened time, / Unfold the evil which is here wrapt up / In countenance.
author: Meas. for Meas

text: Think of the hosts of worlds, and of the plagues in this world-mote—death puts an end to the whole.
author: Carlyle

text: Keep not standing fix'd and rooted; / Briskly venture, briskly roam; / Head and hand, where'er thou foot it, / And stout heart are still at home. / In what land the sun does visit, / Brisk are we, whate'er betide; / To give space for wandering is it / That the world was made so wide.
author: Goethe

text: Mankind at large alway resemble frivolous children; they are impatient of thought, and wish to be amused.
author: Emerson

text: It is with ideas as with pieces of money; those of least value generally circulate the best.
author: Punch

text: While craving justice for ourselves, it is never wise to be unjust to others.
author: Lew Wallace

text: Genius believes its faintest presentiment against the testimony of all history, for it knows that facts are not ultimates, but that a state of mind is the ancestor of everything.
author: Emerson

text: No man is born into this world whose work is not born with him; there is always work, and tools to work withal, for those who will; and blessed are the horny hands of toil.
author: Lowell

text: Take no thought for the morrow; for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself.
author: Jesus

text: The less men think the more they talk.
author: Montesquieu

text: When a writer sets to work again after a long pause, his faculties have, as it were, to be caught in the field and brought in and harnessed.
author: Froude

text: Thou wilt never sell thy life, or any part of thy life, in a satisfactory manner. Give it like a royal heart; let the price of it be nothing; then hast thou in a certain sense got all for it.
author: Carlyle

text: No thought is contented. The better sort, / As thoughts of things divine, are intermixed / With scruples, and do set the word itself / Against the word.
author: Rich. II

text: A truth / Looks freshest in the fashion of the day.
author: Tennyson

text: Stern accuracy in inquiring, bold imagination in expounding and filling up, these are the two pinions on which history soars—or flutters and wabbles.
author: Carlyle

text: Ridicule is a weak weapon when levelled at a strong mind; but common men are cowards, and dread an empty laugh.
author: Tupper

text: Try for yourselves what you can read in half-an-hour, ... and consider what treasures you might have laid by at the end of the year; and what happiness, fortitude and wisdom they would have given you during all the days of your life.
author: John Morley

text: All pleasure must be bought at the price of pain.
author: John Foster

text: Ye gentlemen of England / That live at home at ease, / Ah! little do you think upon / The dangers of the seas.
author: Martyn Parker

text: A consistent man believes in destiny, a capricious man in chance.
author: Disraeli

text: Shakespeare wrote perfect historical plays on subjects belonging to the preceding centuries, they are perfect plays just because there is no care about centuries in them, but a life which all men recognise for the human life of all time; ... a rogue in the fifteenth century being, at heart, what a rogue is in the nineteenth and was in the twelfth; and an honest or a knightly man being, in like manner, very similar to other such at any other time.
author: Ruskin

text: Three things that enrich genius are contentment of mind, the cherishing of good thoughts, and the exercise of memory.
author: Southey

text: Generally all warlike people are a little idle, and love danger better than travail.
author: Bacon

text: Zeal without knowledge is like expedition to a man in the dark.
author: Newton

text: In Nature things move violently to their places, and calmly in their place; so virtue in ambition is violent, in authority settled and calm.
author: Bacon

text: Quotations from profane authors, cold allusions, false pathetic, antitheses and hyperboles, are out of doors.
author: La Bruyère

text: Remembrance wakes with all her busy train, / Swells at my breast, and turns the past to pain.
author: Goldsmith

text: Redlichkeit gedeiht in jedem Stande
author: Schiller

text: This present is a ruinous and ruining world.
author: Carlyle

text: Best men are moulded out of faults.
author: Meas. for Meas

text: Life is act, and not to do is death.
author: Lewis Morris

text: Nothing in love can be premeditated; it is as a power divine, that thinks and feels within us, unswathed by our control.
author: Mme. de Staël

text: Flour cannot be sown and seed-corn ought not to be ground.
author: Goethe

text: Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus, and we petty men / Walk under his huge legs and peep about / To find ourselves dishonourable graves.
author: Jul. Cæs
